item.title: Running an enterprise MCP registry: a playbook for governed tool discovery
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: The official MCP Registry is designed to feed subregistries. A playbook for running a private enterprise MCP registry: curation, namespaces, approvals and client rollout.
item.content:encoded:
Once a few teams adopt MCP, the question shifts from 'how do I build a server?' to 'which servers are we allowed to use?'. The MCP Registry was designed with that in mind: a public upstream that organisations can mirror, filter and extend with their own private servers.

A typical enterprise MCP adoption follows a pattern. A few engineers connect assistants to useful servers. A platform team builds internal servers for the CRM, the data warehouse and the ticketing system. Within months there are dozens of servers, nobody knows which are approved, and security finds a community server with broad file system access on a developer laptop. The fix is not to ban MCP. It is to give people a catalogue of servers they're allowed to use.

How the MCP Registry is designed

The official MCP Registry launched in preview in September 2025 as an open catalogue of publicly available servers14. Three design choices matter for enterprises:

  • Metadata, not code. Entries describe servers and point to packages in existing registries such as npm, PyPI and Docker Hub12.
  • Verified namespaces. Server names use a reverse-DNS format, such as io.github.username/server or com.example/server, tied to a verified GitHub account or domain2. That gives you a basis for trusting who published what.
  • Built to be extended. The registry and its API specification are open source, so others can build compatible subregistries that pull from it, filter it and add their own servers13.

The registry remains in preview, and its documentation warns that breaking changes or data resets may occur before general availability2. Build against it, but pin and mirror what you depend on.

The playbook

1. Decide what "approved" means

Write down the criteria before choosing tools: publisher verified, source available, package signed or pinned, permissions documented, data classification of what it touches, and an internal owner. The controls in securing MCP servers make a good starting checklist.

2. Stand up a private subregistry

Run a registry that implements the same API, so clients that understand the official registry can use yours35. Servers on internal hostnames or private package feeds belong here, not in the public registry2.

3. Mirror, don't proxy

Pull public entries into a staging area, review them, then promote approved versions. Pin to specific package versions so an upstream update can't change what your users run without review. This is the same discipline as AI supply chain security.

4. Enrich entries with your context

Add what the public registry can't know: owner, data classification, allowed user groups, required auth extension, and a link to the review record. Tool annotations and UI capabilities, covered in MCP Apps and tool annotations, should be part of the review.

5. Point clients at it

Configure managed IDEs and assistants to discover servers from your registry, and where clients support it, block unapproved sources. A catalogue nobody is pointed at is just documentation.

6. Tie it to identity

Approval should map to who can use a server. Pair the registry with the enterprise authorisation patterns in MCP extensions, so access is granted through your identity provider rather than per-server credentials.

7. Measure and prune

Track which servers are used, by whom and how often, using the telemetry approach in LLM observability. Retire servers without owners or usage, and re-review on major version changes.

A registry turns MCP from a collection of personal integrations into a platform. The governance lives in the promotion step, not the protocol.

Common mistakes

  • Treating the public registry as an allow-list. Listing proves a verified namespace, not safety.
  • Floating versions. "Latest" from upstream means unreviewed code on every laptop.
  • No owner per server. Internal servers without owners become the next unpatched dependency.
  • Registry without enforcement. If clients can still add any server, the registry is advisory only.

item.title: The UAE's new Federal Authority for AI and Data: what it means for technology teams
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: The UAE has merged its AI office, digital government and data office into one federal authority. What has been announced, what is still unknown, and how I'd prepare.
item.content:encoded:
In June 2026 the UAE created a single federal body for AI, data governance and digital government. This week Dubai set new targets for its AI campus. For companies building or selling AI in the Emirates, the institutional map is consolidating, and that changes who sets the standards you'll be measured against.

For years, AI and data policy in the UAE was spread across several bodies: an AI office within the federal government, the digital government function inside the telecoms regulator, a data office, and emirate-level and free zone authorities alongside them. Teams working here learned to ask "which regulator?" before "which rule?". That is starting to change.

This is an architect's reading of public announcements and law firm commentary, not legal advice.

What was announced

In June 2026 the UAE approved the establishment of the Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data, reporting to the Cabinet, as a unified national body for data governance, artificial intelligence and digital government12. Commentary reports that it brings together three existing functions13:

Previous bodyWhat it covered
Artificial Intelligence OfficeNational AI strategy and programmes
TDRA Information and Digital Government SectorFederal digital government services and standards
Emirates Data OfficeNational data governance

The mandate described in commentary covers the national AI strategy, government data governance, and standards and compliance across federal entities13. By October, reporting on the UAE's AI programme was already framing the authority as the body bringing national data, AI and digital government systems together6.

This week: Dubai's AI campus targets

On 26 October, during the Dubai AI Festival, Dubai approved new targets for its AI campus: more than 1,000 AI companies and over 5,000 specialised jobs by 203045. Together with federal consolidation, the direction is clear: one national voice on AI and data standards, and emirate-level competition to host the companies building on them.

Consolidation usually means fewer, clearer standards, applied more consistently. Teams that have been relying on ambiguity should plan for less of it.

What we don't know yet

  • Private sector reach. The described mandate centres on federal entities. How far its standards will extend to private companies, directly or through procurement, is not yet clear.
  • Interaction with free zones. DIFC and ADGM have their own data protection regimes, including DIFC Regulation 10 on AI systems. How federal AI standards will sit alongside them remains to be seen.
  • Data protection supervision. The federal PDPL continues to apply. Which body leads on its AI-related aspects will become clearer through guidance.
  • Health data. Sector rules, such as those in the UAE health data law, remain in place.

The regional pattern

Saudi Arabia went down this path earlier, with the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority as a single body for data and AI7, alongside its own data protection law covered in Saudi PDPL and cross-border AI. A combined data and AI authority tends to treat data governance and AI governance as one discipline. Architecturally, that's right: most AI risk is data risk.

How I'd prepare

  1. Map your current obligations by entity and location: federal PDPL, free zone regimes, sector rules, and where your models and data actually run, as discussed in UAE AI infrastructure.
  2. Build governance on a recognised framework, such as ISO 42001 or the NIST AI RMF, so national standards become a mapping exercise.
  3. If you sell to government, expect federal data and AI standards to appear in procurement first. Keep an AI system inventory and data lineage ready to evidence.
  4. Unify data and AI governance internally. If the regulator treats them as one discipline, a separate AI committee disconnected from data owners will struggle.
  5. Watch for guidance from the new authority and plan a quarterly review of your mapping.

item.title: SKOS or OWL? Choosing the right model for enterprise taxonomies and ontologies
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: SKOS and OWL are both W3C standards for knowledge models, and they solve different problems. When to use each, how to combine them, and the most common enterprise mistake.
item.content:encoded:
Enterprise ontology programmes often stall on a modelling question disguised as a tooling one: should the product taxonomy, the risk register or the clinical code list be an OWL ontology or a SKOS vocabulary? The answer is usually both, for different jobs.

Every organisation already has knowledge models. They're in spreadsheets of product categories, SharePoint term stores, code lists in the data warehouse and the folder structure of the document system. When an ontology or knowledge graph programme starts, one of the first decisions is how to represent these formally. Two W3C standards dominate the conversation, and choosing the wrong one for a given job is a common reason programmes lose a year.

Two standards, two purposes

SKOS, the Simple Knowledge Organization System, became a W3C Recommendation in 2009. It is a common data model for sharing and linking knowledge organisation systems, such as thesauri, taxonomies and classification schemes, on the web1. Its world is concepts, labels and loose relations between them.

OWL 2, the Web Ontology Language, defines classes, properties and logical axioms that reasoners can use to infer new facts and detect contradictions. Its profiles, finalised in their second edition in 2012, trade expressiveness for tractable reasoning3.

The SKOS designers were explicit that SKOS was not meant to compete with OWL but to complement it, offering a path to bring existing knowledge that doesn't map easily into an OWL ontology onto the semantic web5.

Side by side

SKOSOWL 2
Core unitConcept with labelsClass, property, individual
Hierarchyskos:broader: "is filed under", for navigation and retrievalrdfs:subClassOf: "every X is a Y", logical subsumption
LabelsFirst-class: preferred, alternative and hidden labels, with at most one preferred label per language1Annotations, not part of the logic
ReasoningLight; little to inferRich, with profiles tuned for scale3
Cross-scheme linksMapping properties such as exact, close and broader matches1Equivalence and subclass axioms with logical consequences
Who maintains itTaxonomists, subject experts, business ownersOntologists and data architects
Best forProduct categories, subject tags, code lists, synonyms for searchDomain models, constraints, integration semantics

The mistake that matters most

The most expensive error is treating a taxonomy hierarchy as a class hierarchy. In a product catalogue, "Garden furniture" sits under "Outdoor" and also under "Furniture". That is a filing decision, not a claim that every garden chair is, logically, an instance of "Outdoor".

SKOS is careful here. skos:broader is used only for direct hierarchical links and is not declared transitive; skos:broaderTransitive is a separate superproperty for inferring indirect links12. Converting the same hierarchy into rdfs:subClassOf makes every relation logically binding, and a reasoner will happily draw conclusions nobody intended.

If the business owner would say "it's filed under", use SKOS. If they would say "it is always a kind of", consider OWL. Most enterprise hierarchies are the first.

Choosing OWL profiles when you do need logic

Where OWL is the right tool, its profiles help match reasoning to scale34:

  • OWL 2 EL suits ontologies with very large numbers of classes and properties, with polynomial-time reasoning for core tasks. Large biomedical terminologies are the classic fit.
  • OWL 2 QL targets large volumes of instance data queried through relational databases, which suits virtual knowledge graphs over existing warehouses.
  • OWL 2 RL supports rule-based reasoning that works directly on RDF triples, practical inside many triple stores.

Choosing a profile early prevents a common failure: a model that is logically elegant and unusable at production volume.

The combined pattern I use

  1. A small OWL core for the domain: customer, product, contract, patient, asset, and the relations between them. Keep it in a tractable profile.
  2. SKOS vocabularies for classification: product categories, risk types, diagnosis groupings, document subjects. Instances in the core point to concepts through ordinary properties, such as "has category".
  3. Mappings between vocabularies using SKOS mapping properties, so a local code list can align with an industry standard without pretending they are identical.
  4. SHACL for data quality, as described in SHACL validation, because closed-world checks belong outside the open-world logic of OWL.
  5. Labels feed search and AI. SKOS alternative and hidden labels give retrieval and GraphRAG the synonyms and misspellings users actually type.

This also clarifies ownership. Business teams can maintain vocabularies in a taxonomy tool without touching the ontology, while architects govern the core. How these pieces relate to a semantic layer is covered in ontology vs knowledge graph vs semantic layer, and how clinical vocabularies are handled in practice in clinical terminologies in OMOP.

How I can help

item.title: SMART on FHIR for AI apps: an authorisation checklist for clinical data access
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: AI apps that read EHR data need SMART on FHIR authorisation done properly. A checklist covering v2 granular scopes, PKCE, backend services and agent access to clinical data.
item.content:encoded:
Ambient scribes, chart summarisers and clinical agents all need to read and sometimes write EHR data. SMART on FHIR is how they should get that access. The hard questions in a health AI security review are usually about scopes, launch context and token handling, not the model.

A health AI product usually starts with a demo against a sandbox and a broad token. Then it meets a hospital's security review. The questions are rarely about the model. They are about which data the app can reach, on whose behalf, for how long, and how anyone would know if it reached further than it should.

SMART on FHIR answers most of those questions if it is used properly. This checklist is what I work through when designing or reviewing EHR access for AI applications.

Why it matters more for AI

Traditional SMART apps show data to a clinician who is already authorised to see it. AI apps often do more: summarise a whole record, draft notes back into the chart, or run in the background across many patients. That widens both the data an app touches and the consequences of a misconfigured scope. In the US, HTI-1 also moved certified health IT from SMART v1 to the SMART App Launch 2.0 guide for the standardised patient and population API criterion, so v2 behaviour is now the baseline buyers expect6. The policy side is covered in HTI-1 to HTI-5.

1. Scopes: ask for the least, precisely

  • Use v2 scope syntax. Permissions are expressed as suffixes from c, r, u, d and s. patient/Observation.rs grants read and search on the patient's observations; patient/Observation.cu grants create and update1.
  • Narrow with search parameters. v2 allows granular scopes such as Observation access limited to the vital-signs category15. A sepsis model that only needs vitals and labs shouldn't hold a token for psychotherapy notes.
  • Prefer patient/ over user/ and system/ wherever the use case is about one patient in context.
  • Separate read and write. If the AI drafts notes, consider a distinct, reviewable write path rather than giving the summariser create rights.
  • Check what the server actually supports. Servers advertise capabilities in their SMART configuration5; don't assume granular scopes are enforced everywhere.

2. Launch and token handling

  • PKCE with S256, always. The specification says all SMART apps shall support PKCE, servers shall support S256 and shall not support the plain method2.
  • Use EHR launch for in-workflow AI, so the patient and encounter come from the EHR's launch context, not from parameters the app constructs12.
  • Request openid fhirUser so every AI action can be attributed to an identified user2.
  • Keep tokens out of the model. Access tokens belong in the integration layer, never in prompts, logs or tool arguments the model can see or echo.
  • Be deliberate about offline access. Refresh tokens extend reach well beyond the clinician's session; request them only when the use case needs it.

The model should never hold a credential. It asks a tool for data; the tool holds the token, enforces scope and logs the call.

3. Background and population workloads

  • Use SMART Backend Services for autonomous processing, such as overnight risk scoring or quality measures. It is designed for clients with pre-authorised scopes and no user in the loop3.
  • Authenticate with asymmetric keys. private_key_jwt is the specification's preferred method because no shared secret crosses the wire; clients must support RS384 and ES3844.
  • Rotate keys through a JWKS endpoint, and treat the private key with the same controls as any production secret.
  • Use bulk export for volume, as in FHIR bulk data pipelines, rather than looping single-patient queries.

4. Agents and tools

  • One tool, one scope set. If an agent reaches FHIR through MCP servers, each server should hold the narrowest token for its job, with the controls in securing MCP servers.
  • Keep patient context fixed. An agent must not be able to switch patients by changing a tool argument; patient identity comes from the launch, not the prompt. This is a key defence against prompt injection.
  • Human approval for writes. Drafted notes, orders or messages go to a clinician for review before they are committed, as in ambient scribe architectures.

5. Evidence for the security review

  • A table of every scope requested, why, and which feature uses it.
  • Audit logs linking each FHIR call to user, patient, feature and model version.
  • Token lifetimes, refresh policy and revocation procedure.
  • Results of testing with a SMART conformance tool against the target servers.
  • A data flow showing exactly where PHI goes, including any model provider, mapped to HIPAA Security Rule controls.

item.title: In-place Pod resize on Kubernetes: field notes for right-sizing without restarts
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: In-place Pod resize is stable in Kubernetes 1.35, letting CPU and memory change without recreating Pods. How it works, where it bites, and how I'd use it to cut cost.
item.content:encoded:
For years, changing a Pod's CPU or memory meant replacing the Pod. That made right-sizing disruptive, so most teams over-provisioned and left it there. With in-place resize stable since Kubernetes 1.35, the excuse is gone. The operational details still matter.

Almost every Kubernetes cost review finds the same thing: requests set generously at launch and never touched again. Teams know the numbers are wrong. They leave them because changing them used to mean rolling every Pod, and nobody wants to explain a restart to a stateful service, a long-running batch job or a model server that takes minutes to warm up.

That constraint has gone. These are notes on what changed and how I would put it to work.

What changed

In-place Pod resize arrived as alpha in Kubernetes 1.27, reached beta in 1.33 and graduated to stable in 1.3513. It makes CPU and memory requests and limits mutable on a running Pod. You send the change to the Pod's resize subresource, for example with kubectl patch --subresource resize, which needs kubectl 1.32 or later2.

Each container declares a resizePolicy per resource. NotRequired asks for the change to be applied without a restart; RestartContainer restarts that container to apply it. A common pattern in the documentation is CPU set to NotRequired and memory set to RestartContainer2.

The stable release added two things operators will notice. Memory limits can now be decreased, with the kubelet only allowing it when current usage is below the new limit, a best-effort check rather than a guarantee. And when a node can't fit every pending resize, retries are ordered by PriorityClass, then QoS class, then how long the request has waited1.

Watch the conditions, not just the spec

A resize is a request, not a guarantee. The kubelet reports progress through Pod conditions2:

ConditionReasonMeaning
PodResizePendingDeferredDoesn't fit now, might fit later; the kubelet keeps retrying
PodResizePendingInfeasibleCan never fit on this node as it stands
PodResizeInProgress(none) or ErrorAccepted and being applied; errors in actuation surface here

The practical rule: alert on long-lived PodResizePending. A spec that says 4 CPUs while the container still runs on 2 is a quiet source of confusion in incidents and cost reports alike.

The spec says what you asked for. The status says what you got. Right-sizing dashboards should read the status.

Where the VPA fits

The Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommends requests from observed usage and applies them. Its InPlaceOrRecreate update mode tries an in-place resize first and falls back to recreating the Pod when that isn't possible; the 1.35 release blog described that mode as graduating to beta15.

This is the combination that changes cost economics. Recommendations used to sit in a report because applying them was disruptive. With in-place updates they can be applied continuously, within limits you set.

Pod-level resources are next

Kubernetes 1.36 promoted in-place resize of Pod-level resources to beta, meaning a shared budget for all containers in a Pod can also change without recreating it4. That is useful for Pods with sidecars, where per-container numbers are hard to tune separately. I would treat it as beta: pilot it, but don't build a platform default on it yet.

Where it bites

  • Applications that size themselves at start-up. A runtime that reads its memory limit once, such as a JVM heap or a worker pool sized to CPU count, won't notice a change. For those, a restart policy on memory is the honest choice.
  • Memory decreases. The usage check is best-effort, so shrinking memory on a busy Pod still carries OOM risk1. Shrink gradually and watch.
  • Node fragmentation. Growing in place only works if the node has room. Busy nodes produce Deferred resizes; plan headroom or accept fallback to recreation.
  • Quotas and policy. Resizes still count against namespace quotas, and teams will need guardrails on how far they can go, enforced with admission policies in multi-tenant clusters.

How I'd roll it out

  1. Measure first. Compare requests with real usage by namespace and team, using the allocation approach in FOCUS-based cost allocation.
  2. Start with CPU on stateless services, using NotRequired, where the risk is lowest and the savings show quickly.
  3. Run the VPA in recommendation mode for a few weeks, then enable InPlaceOrRecreate on workloads that tolerate the fallback.
  4. Use it for warm-up spikes. Services that need extra CPU at start-up, including model servers like those in vLLM serving, can start large and shrink once warm.
  5. Alert on pending resizes and report status, not spec, in cost dashboards.
  6. Combine with scale-to-zero from Kubernetes FinOps: horizontal scaling for traffic shape, vertical for per-Pod fit.

item.title: Text-to-SQL agents need a semantic layer, not just a bigger model
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: LLMs ace text-to-SQL demos and stumble on real enterprise schemas. What Spider 2.0 showed, why a governed semantic layer helps, and how I design data access for AI agents.
item.content:encoded:
'Ask your data anything' is one of the most requested AI features, and one of the most disappointing in production. The demo works on a tidy schema. The real warehouse has thousands of columns, conflicting definitions and tribal knowledge. Research and the market are converging on the same fix.

Every data team has seen the demo: a business user types "what was revenue by region last quarter?" and the model writes perfect SQL. Then the same tool meets the real warehouse, with three tables that could be "revenue", a region column that changed meaning in 2023, and a fiscal calendar nobody wrote down. The answers come back quickly, confidently and wrong.

What the research shows

Spider 2.0, presented at ICLR 2025, was built from real enterprise workflows: 632 problems over databases often with more than a thousand columns, in systems such as BigQuery and Snowflake. The authors reported that a strong reasoning model using a code agent framework solved 21.3% of tasks, compared with 91.2% on the earlier Spider 1.0 benchmark and 73.0% on BIRD12.

The gap isn't mainly about SQL syntax. It is about knowing which tables matter, what columns mean, how entities join, and which business rules apply. That knowledge rarely lives in the schema.

Text-to-SQL fails on meaning, not grammar. A bigger model writes more fluent wrong queries; a semantic layer gives it the right things to query.

What a semantic layer gives an agent

A semantic layer defines business concepts, such as metrics, dimensions, entities and their relationships, once, in governed code, and exposes them to every tool. For an AI agent, that changes the task from "write SQL against 1,500 columns" to "pick the governed metric 'net revenue', group by the dimension 'sales region', filter to last fiscal quarter". The layer generates the SQL.

  • Consistency. The agent's answer matches the dashboard, because both use the same definition.
  • Smaller search space. Choosing from a curated set of metrics is far easier than reasoning over raw tables.
  • Governance. Access control, row-level security and certified definitions apply to AI queries just as they do to BI.
  • Explainability. The agent can say which metric and filters it used, in business terms a user can check.

The market is converging

In September 2025 Snowflake, Salesforce, dbt Labs and others announced the Open Semantic Interchange, an initiative for a vendor-neutral semantic model specification, explicitly framed around making data ready for AI3. In October 2025 dbt Labs moved MetricFlow, the engine behind its semantic layer, to the Apache 2.0 licence and said it would align it with that initiative45.

Whatever tools you choose, the direction is clear: business definitions are becoming portable, open artefacts that AI and BI share, rather than logic buried in each dashboard.

Semantic layer, ontology or both?

A semantic layer is optimised for metrics: numbers aggregated over dimensions. An ontology describes entities and relationships more broadly, as I set out in ontology vs knowledge graph vs semantic layer. For "how much" questions, the semantic layer is the right tool. For "which suppliers are connected to this incident", a knowledge graph answers better. Mature data platforms give agents both, with clear guidance on which to use.

How I design data access for AI agents

  1. Start with the twenty questions people actually ask, and define the metrics and dimensions they need in the semantic layer first.
  2. Expose governed tools, not a SQL console. Agents call "query metric" and "list dimensions" tools, for example through MCP servers built with the controls in securing MCP servers.
  3. Return the definition with the answer, so users see which metric, filters and time range were used.
  4. Fall back honestly. If a question can't be answered from governed definitions, say so and route it to an analyst, rather than improvising SQL.
  5. Evaluate with real questions and known answers, as in evaluation sets that predict production, and track accuracy by question type.
  6. Keep definitions under contract, with the change discipline in data contracts, so a schema change can't silently break what agents report.

item.title: MCP extensions: how to adopt them without fragmenting your agent platform
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: MCP extensions add UI, enterprise auth and domain conventions on top of the core protocol. How extensions work, which are official, and how I decide which to adopt in an enterprise.
item.content:encoded:
The Model Context Protocol keeps its core small and grows through extensions: interactive apps, enterprise authorisation, and domain conventions. That's good design. It also means every enterprise now needs a policy on which extensions to support.

Enterprises adopting MCP usually start with the core: clients, servers, tools and resources. Within months, requests arrive for more: interactive interfaces inside the chat, single sign-on instead of per-server logins, machine-to-machine access for batch agents, conventions for regulated data. MCP's answer to all of these is extensions. Understanding how they work is now part of designing an agent platform.

Core, projects and extensions

The MCP maintainers describe the ecosystem in three layers1:

  • The core specification: how clients and servers talk, and the minimum bar for interoperability.
  • Projects: supporting infrastructure such as the Registry for discovering servers and the Inspector for testing.
  • Extensions: optional patterns for specialised needs, built on top of the core.

Extensions are strictly additive. They are negotiated during the initialisation handshake, and a client or server that doesn't recognise one simply skips it, so the baseline protocol keeps working12. They are also how future protocol changes get validated: an extension that gains traction signals what might belong in the core1.

What exists today

CategoryExamplesWhy an enterprise cares
UIMCP Apps, the first official extension, for interactive interfaces in the conversation1Richer workflows; new security review surface. See MCP Apps and tool annotations
AuthorisationOAuth Client Credentials for machine-to-machine access, and Enterprise-Managed Authorization for central identity provider control13Central policy, audit and onboarding through your identity provider
Domain conventionsCommunity groups exploring, for example, compliance metadata for financial services1Shared semantics for regulated workflows, once mature

The maintainers also draw a useful line: proprietary client features that happen to use MCP are not necessarily extensions, and they encourage implementers to adopt extensions as the standard way to add custom behaviour1.

Prefer official extensions over client-specific features. The first works across clients you'll adopt next year; the second ties your workflows to one vendor.

How I decide which to adopt

  1. Is it official, recommended or community-defined? Official extensions live in the MCP organisation and go through the SEP process5. Community extensions can be valuable but carry more change risk.
  2. Which of our clients support it? Check the extension support matrix4 against the clients your organisation actually uses. An extension supported by one client only is a pilot, not a standard.
  3. What's the security impact? UI extensions run code from servers inside hosts; auth extensions change who can access what. Both need review before approval.
  4. Does it degrade gracefully? Because extensions are optional, test what happens when a client doesn't support one. The workflow should still be safe, even if less convenient.
  5. Who owns it internally? Each supported extension needs an owner on the platform team, a version policy and a place in your server review checklist.

Auth extensions first

If you adopt one extension category first, make it authorisation. Per-user, per-server OAuth doesn't scale in an enterprise, and machine-to-machine agents need a supported way to authenticate without a person in the loop. Centralising access through your identity provider gives you consistent policy and one audit trail, which supports the controls in securing MCP servers and the evidence expected in SOC 2.

Contributing back

Organisations in regulated sectors have a real opportunity here. If your industry needs shared conventions, such as provenance, consent or compliance metadata on tool calls, the SEP process offers an Extensions Track for proposing them5. Defining those conventions openly is better than every vendor inventing its own.

item.title: Colorado's AI law reset: what changed in 2026, and what to build regardless
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Colorado's 2024 AI Act was delayed, blocked in court and replaced in 2026 by a narrower notice-based law effective 2027. What changed, and the AI governance worth building anyway.
item.content:encoded:
Colorado passed the first broad US state law on high-risk AI in 2024. By mid-2026 it had been delayed, blocked in federal court and replaced with a narrower notice-based law. For companies selling AI into the US, the lesson goes beyond Colorado.

For two years, the Colorado AI Act was the US law that AI governance teams planned around. It was the first broad state statute aimed at high-risk AI used in consequential decisions such as hiring, lending and housing. Many companies built programmes around its risk management and impact assessment requirements. In 2026 the ground moved.

This is an architect's summary of public commentary, not legal advice. Confirm current obligations with counsel.

What happened

WhenEvent
2024SB 24-205 enacted, originally effective February 2026, requiring deployers of high-risk AI to adopt risk management programmes, run impact assessments and notify consumers1
Aug 2025A special-session bill delayed the effective date to 30 June 202612
Apr 2026A federal court blocked enforcement after a constitutional challenge, with the US Department of Justice intervening in support of the challenge3
May 2026SB 26-189 enacted, repealing and reenacting the framework with a narrower, notice-based approach effective 1 January 202734

What the new law looks like

Commentary describes SB 26-189 as built around automated decision-making technology used in consequential decisions, including employment decisions about Colorado applicants and employees4. The headline change is what it no longer requires: covered employers no longer need risk management programmes or annual impact assessments. Instead, the law focuses on notice and disclosure, specific consumer rights and record retention, with duties split between developers and deployers45. The Attorney General is to adopt implementing rules before it takes effect, so operational details may still change4.

Regulation can lighten. Customer expectations rarely do. Enterprise buyers will keep asking how your AI makes decisions about people, whatever Colorado requires.

The broader lesson

Colorado's path mirrors what has happened elsewhere. The EU delayed parts of its AI Act through the Digital Omnibus. US federal health IT rules proposed removing AI transparency requirements, as covered in HTI-1 to HTI-5. Requirements are moving in different directions in different places, and quickly.

Building a compliance programme around one statute's exact wording is fragile in that environment. Building core governance capabilities that map to several regimes is robust.

What I'd build regardless

  1. An inventory of automated decisions about people: which systems influence hiring, credit, pricing, eligibility or access, and how much weight the AI carries.
  2. Notices generated from the inventory, so disclosures stay accurate as systems change. Notice is the obligation that survived in Colorado, and it is common elsewhere.
  3. Records that can answer "why": inputs, model versions and outputs for consequential decisions, retained for a defined period, using the logging in LLM observability.
  4. A route for people to contest decisions and reach a human.
  5. Testing for bias and quality before release and on a schedule, even where no longer mandated, because it is what customers and courts will ask about. See evaluating AI agents.
  6. A framework to map against, such as those compared in ISO 42001 and the NIST AI RMF, so new state laws become a mapping exercise rather than a new programme.

For companies selling into the US from the Gulf or Europe

For companies selling from the UAE or Europe into US enterprises, the practical answer is one governance core, evidenced well, then mapped to each market: the EU AI Act, US state laws as they settle, and Gulf rules such as DIFC Regulation 10. That's cheaper than chasing each statute separately, and it survives the next reset.

item.title: Zero-code observability with OBI: where OpenTelemetry's eBPF instrumentation fits
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: OBI uses eBPF to capture traces, metrics and log correlation without code changes. What it covers, its 2026 path to 1.0, where it fits beside SDKs, and how I'd roll it out.
item.content:encoded:
Instrumenting every service with an SDK is the gold standard, and the reason many estates have no tracing at all. OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation, OBI, offers traces and metrics without touching application code. It changes how fast you can get visibility, though it doesn't replace SDKs entirely.

Many organisations have tracing on the services built in the last few years and nothing on the rest: the legacy Java monolith, the vendor binary, the Go service whose author left. Instrumenting each one with an SDK means code changes, releases and ownership that often doesn't exist. So the gaps stay, and incidents in those gaps take longest to resolve.

What OBI does

OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation uses eBPF to inspect application executables and the operating system's networking layer, capturing trace spans, rate-errors-duration metrics, runtime metrics and service relationships for supported Linux workloads, without modifying application code or configuration1. The documentation lists support for languages including Java, .NET, Go, Python, Ruby, Node.js, C, C++ and Rust, visibility into TLS traffic without decryption, context propagation across services, and configuration-free auto-instrumentation on Kubernetes1.

That last point matters most in practice. On a cluster, you can get a baseline service map and latency metrics for everything in days, not quarters.

Log correlation without touching the app

A recent addition addresses a common incident pain: you have a failing trace, but no way to find the matching log lines because the service never added trace context to its logs. OBI can now add trace and span IDs to logs written to stdout or stderr, because through eBPF it knows which request each thread is serving at the moment of the write3.

The boundaries are stated clearly: it applies to stdout and stderr, only annotates lines written while OBI has active trace context, needs elevated privileges, and on older kernels only some write paths are enriched; the common write path needs Linux 6.0 or later. It also needs a small change in the log pipeline3.

eBPF instrumentation is the fastest way to remove blind spots. SDKs are the way to add meaning. Most mature estates will want both.

Where it's heading in 2026

The OBI SIG's 2026 goals centre on a stable 1.0 release for production readiness, with complete configuration documentation, adoption of OpenTelemetry's declarative configuration and telemetry schemas, and test coverage targets. They also plan to expand protocols to messaging systems such as MQTT, AMQP, NATS and Redis pub/sub, extend database support, instrument cloud service SDKs, broaden .NET support, and strengthen integration with OpenTelemetry SDKs for hybrid instrumentation2.

Check the project's current release status before production rollout4, and pilot in non-critical environments first, in line with the stability approach in OpenTelemetry's stable-by-default push.

OBI or SDK?

OBI (eBPF)OpenTelemetry SDKs
Code changesNoneRequired
Coverage speedWhole cluster quicklyService by service
Business contextLimited to protocol-level dataCustom spans, attributes and events
PrivilegesElevated, node-levelRuns inside the application
Best forBaselines, legacy and third-party servicesCore services where detail matters

How I'd roll it out

  1. Start with the blind spots. Deploy OBI where SDK instrumentation is missing, and compare the service map with what teams believe the architecture is.
  2. Route through your Collector gateway, as in Collector deployment patterns, so sampling, redaction and export are handled centrally.
  3. Review privileges with security. eBPF instrumentation runs with elevated access on nodes; treat it as platform infrastructure with the same controls as other node-level agents, enforced through admission policies.
  4. Check data sensitivity. Capturing protocol data, including from encrypted traffic, can expose sensitive values. Configure what is collected and redact at the gateway.
  5. Add SDKs where business context matters, such as checkout flows, AI calls with GenAI attributes, and regulated workflows.
  6. Watch cardinality and cost, since cluster-wide instrumentation can generate a lot of telemetry quickly.

item.title: Clinical prediction models on OMOP: how to build models that work beyond one hospital
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Many clinical prediction models are never validated beyond their own data. How OHDSI patient-level prediction defines problems, measures performance and validates externally.
item.content:encoded:
Clinical prediction is one of the oldest uses of machine learning in healthcare, and one of the most disappointing in practice. Models that look excellent at one hospital often fail at the next. OHDSI's patient-level prediction framework is a practical answer.

Risk scores for readmission, sepsis, deterioration or medication harm are some of the most requested clinical AI projects. They are also among the easiest to get wrong. A model trained on one hospital's data, evaluated on a random split of the same data, and published with a strong AUC, often performs noticeably worse somewhere else, or even in the same hospital a year later.

The OHDSI community has spent years building a standard way to do this better. Its approach is useful even if you never touch the OHDSI tools.

The problem with most prediction models

The Book of OHDSI is direct about it: many published patient-level prediction efforts don't follow model development guidelines, fail to perform extensive external validation, or provide too few details for others to reproduce and validate them1. It points to the TRIPOD reporting guideline as a standard for transparent reporting14.

The underlying issue is that a model learns the habits of the data it was trained on: coding practices, patient mix, documentation patterns. Those don't travel.

Define the problem precisely

OHDSI frames every prediction problem in the same form: among a target cohort, who will go on to have an outcome within a time-at-risk? Prediction happens at a defined moment, and only information from the observation window before that moment may be used1.

The same template covers disease onset, treatment response, safety and adherence. The book's examples include predicting ischaemic stroke among newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation patients, and gastrointestinal bleeding among new users of warfarin1. Because target and outcome are standard cohort definitions, another site can rebuild exactly the same problem on its own data.

Most prediction projects fail at the first step: an ambiguous index date. If you can't say precisely when the prediction is made, you can't validate it anywhere else.

Measure the right things

Discrimination, usually summarised by the area under the ROC curve, measures whether the model ranks patients who will have the outcome above those who won't. The book notes that for rare outcomes even a model with a high AUC may not be practical, because many false positives can accompany each true one1.

Calibration measures whether predicted risks match reality: of a hundred patients given a 10% risk, about ten should have the outcome1. In the book's worked example, a model was well calibrated overall but poorly calibrated for younger patients1. Overall metrics hide that kind of problem, which is why subgroup checks matter for both safety and fairness.

Validate externally, always

The book distinguishes internal validation, testing on held-out data from the same database, from external validation, developing in one database and evaluating in another. It recommends always performing external validation on as many new datasets as feasible, because different databases represent different populations, health systems and data capture1.

This is where a common data model pays off. A model built on OMOP can be shared as a package and evaluated at other OMOP sites without moving patient data, which is the federated approach described in federated health analytics. The PatientLevelPrediction R package implements this end to end, from data extraction with standard covariates to training and validation23.

How I'd run a clinical prediction project

  1. Write the prediction question in the standard form and agree it with clinicians before touching data.
  2. Build cohorts on OMOP, checked with data quality tools, so the design is portable.
  3. Start with simple models. Regularised logistic regression is often competitive and easier to explain.
  4. Report discrimination and calibration, overall and by key subgroups, following TRIPOD.
  5. Validate on at least one external dataset before any clinical use.
  6. Plan deployment and monitoring: how the score reaches clinicians, how drift is detected, and how changes are controlled. The transparency practices in HTI-1 to HTI-5 and FDA PCCPs apply.

item.title: Choosing an embedding model for RAG: a checklist that goes beyond the leaderboard
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Embedding choice quietly decides RAG quality, cost and portability. What MTEB and MMTEB measure, why no model wins everything, and the checklist I use to pick and re-evaluate embeddings.
item.content:encoded:
Teams spend weeks choosing an LLM and minutes choosing an embedding model. Yet the embedding model decides what retrieval can find, and changing it later means re-embedding everything. It deserves a more careful decision.

In many RAG systems, the embedding model was chosen because it was the default in a tutorial, or because it topped a leaderboard on the day someone looked. Then retrieval quality disappoints, and the team tunes prompts and chunk sizes for weeks without suspecting the component that decides what can be found at all.

What the benchmarks tell you

The Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, MTEB, evaluates embedding models across many tasks, such as retrieval, classification, clustering and semantic similarity, over dozens of datasets and many languages. Its central finding when published was that no single method dominated across all tasks1. Its multilingual successor, MMTEB, presented at ICLR 2025, expanded to over 500 evaluation tasks across hundreds of languages, including long-document and code retrieval2. Notably, its authors reported that the best-performing publicly available model at the time was a relatively small multilingual model of around 560 million parameters2.

Two lessons follow. Model size isn't the same as fitness for your task. And an average score across hundreds of tasks may hide poor performance on the one task you care about.

Use the leaderboard to build a shortlist, never to make the decision. Your documents, your queries and your languages are the only benchmark that matters.

The checklist

  1. Filter by the task that matters. For RAG, look at retrieval scores, not the overall average. If you search code or long documents, look at those categories specifically.
  2. Check your languages. For Gulf and multilingual products, test Arabic and mixed-language queries explicitly. Many models are strongest in English, and a good average can hide weak Arabic retrieval.
  3. Check domain fit. Clinical, legal and financial language behave differently from web text. Test with real domain documents; if results are weak, hybrid keyword and vector search often helps more than switching models, as in hybrid search for RAG.
  4. Measure on your own data. Build a labelled set of queries and the documents that should be retrieved for them, and measure recall and ranking quality for each candidate. The open-source mteb package can help run standard tasks alongside your own4, and the wider method is in evaluation sets that predict production.
  5. Consider dimensions and cost. Bigger vectors cost more to store and search. Models trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning let you truncate embeddings to smaller sizes with limited quality loss; the original paper reported up to 14 times smaller embeddings at the same accuracy on an image classification benchmark3. Test the trade-off on your own retrieval set.
  6. Consider where it runs. Hosted embedding APIs send your documents to a third party. For regulated or residency-bound data, a self-hosted open model may be necessary, as discussed in Saudi PDPL and cross-border AI and private LLMs on-prem.
  7. Check licence and longevity. If a provider deprecates a model, you must re-embed everything. Prefer models you can keep running, or plan for migration.
  8. Check context length. Some models truncate long inputs silently. Make sure your chunk sizes fit the model's limit.

Plan for re-embedding from day one

Whatever you choose, you will change it eventually: a better model appears, a provider retires one, or your content shifts language or domain. Design for that:

  • Store the model name and version with every vector, and never mix vectors from different models in one index.
  • Keep source text and chunking reproducible, so you can re-embed without re-ingesting.
  • Build new indexes alongside old ones, compare retrieval quality on your evaluation set, and switch traffic only when the new one wins.
  • Budget the cost. Re-embedding a large corpus takes real compute and time; estimate it before you need it.

Where embeddings sit in the bigger picture

Embeddings are one part of retrieval. Reranking, hybrid search, metadata filters and good chunking often matter as much. Where your vectors live is its own decision, covered in pgvector or a vector database. And for some questions, a knowledge graph or GraphRAG beats any embedding, as in GraphRAG vs vector RAG. The most reliable systems treat the embedding model as a swappable, versioned component, chosen with evidence and re-evaluated regularly.

item.title: Kubernetes multi-tenancy: namespaces, virtual control planes or dedicated clusters?
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Sharing Kubernetes clusters saves money but raises isolation questions. How I choose between namespace-per-tenant, virtual control planes and dedicated clusters, using the official guidance.
item.content:encoded:
Every growing platform faces the same question: one cluster per team or customer, or shared clusters with careful isolation? Kubernetes has no built-in concept of a tenant, so the answer is a set of design choices. Here is how I make them.

Clusters multiply quietly. One per team, one per environment, one for that big customer, one for the data science group. Each brings its own upgrades, monitoring, security patches and idle capacity. Eventually someone asks whether all of this could share fewer clusters, and the answer depends almost entirely on who the tenants are and how much they trust each other.

Two kinds of tenancy

The Kubernetes documentation distinguishes two broad use cases1:

  • Multiple teams in one organisation share a cluster. There is some trust between them, members often have direct access through tools or GitOps, and workloads frequently talk to each other.
  • Multiple customers, where a vendor runs workload instances per customer. Customers never touch the cluster, cost matters a great deal, and isolation must be strong.

The documentation also cautions that "hard" and "soft" multi-tenancy are better seen as a spectrum than two categories. Hard multi-tenancy usually describes tenants that don't trust each other, which demands particular attention to data-plane isolation1.

The building blocks

Control plane isolation stops tenants seeing or changing each other's API resources. Namespaces scope names and many policies; RBAC enforces least privilege, which the docs call the most important type of control-plane isolation, because a tenant who can modify another's resources can disable every other protection12. Resource quotas cap what each namespace can consume5.

Data plane isolation protects workloads at runtime: network policies to restrict traffic3, storage isolation, sandboxed containers using virtual machines or userspace kernels for untrusted code, and node isolation that dedicates nodes to a tenant1.

Fairness matters too. API Priority and Fairness prevents one tenant's controllers from overwhelming the API server4.

Containers share a kernel. If tenants may run code you don't trust, namespaces alone are not a security boundary; plan for sandboxing, dedicated nodes or separate clusters.

The three models compared

Namespace per tenantVirtual control plane per tenantCluster per tenant
IsolationShared API server; depends on careful policySeparate API views, including non-namespaced resourcesStrongest; nothing shared but the provider
CostNegligible overheadSomewhat higherHighest, especially on-premises
LimitationsNon-namespaced resources such as CRDs, storage classes and webhooks are sharedCross-tenant sharing is harderOperational overhead per cluster
Best forInternal teams with some trustTenants needing their own CRDs or admin rightsUntrusted tenants, regulated data, residency

This follows the documentation's own description: namespace isolation is well supported with negligible resource cost but can be difficult to configure and doesn't cover non-namespaced resources, while control plane virtualisation isolates those at the cost of somewhat higher resource use1.

How I decide

  1. Who writes code that runs? If tenants can run arbitrary code, assume it may be hostile, and favour sandboxing, dedicated nodes or clusters.
  2. Do tenants need cluster-level resources? Teams that ship their own operators and CRDs push towards virtual control planes.
  3. What do regulators and contracts require? Data residency and customer contracts may require dedicated infrastructure in a region, as in UAE health data localisation.
  4. What can the platform team operate? Fifty clusters run badly are riskier than five run well.
  5. Mix models. Shared clusters for most tenants, dedicated ones for the few that need them, mirroring the hybrid pattern in multi-tenant SaaS on MongoDB.

Practical rules for shared clusters

  • A namespace per workload, with names unique across the whole fleet, which the docs recommend so you can move between shared and dedicated clusters later1.
  • Default-deny networking, with explicit allows.
  • Quotas and limit ranges on every tenant namespace.
  • Guardrails as policy, such as the CEL policies in Kubernetes admission policies, so tenants can't weaken their own isolation.
  • Cost allocation by tenant, using labels and the approaches in Kubernetes FinOps.
  • Separate GPU pools where AI workloads from different tenants compete, with the scheduling controls in gang scheduling.

How I can help

item.title: AI agent memory: what to remember, how to retrieve it, and when to forget
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Agents that remember users and past work are more useful and riskier. What MemGPT, Generative Agents and LongMemEval teach about memory design, and the architecture and governance I use.
item.content:encoded:
An assistant that forgets everything between sessions feels shallow. One that remembers everything becomes slow, confused and a privacy liability. Designing memory is about choosing what deserves to persist, and research gives useful guidance.

The most common complaint about AI assistants in the workplace is that they don't remember. You explain your role, your project and your preferences, and the next day you explain them again. The obvious fix, keeping everything, creates different problems: slower and more expensive responses, answers based on stale information, and a growing store of personal data nobody designed for.

Memory is an architecture decision, not a feature toggle.

Why "keep everything in context" fails

Stuffing history into the prompt runs into the limits covered in long context or RAG: cost and latency grow with every token, and models use long inputs unevenly. Chroma's research found performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows, even on simple tasks4.

LongMemEval, a benchmark presented at ICLR 2025, tested exactly this for assistants. Its 500 questions probe five abilities: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention, embedded in long user-assistant histories. The authors reported that commercial chat assistants and long-context models showed about a 30% accuracy drop when recalling information across sustained interactions3.

Two of those abilities deserve attention. Knowledge updates: when a user changes their address or a project changes scope, memory must reflect the latest truth, not the first. Abstention: when the assistant doesn't know, it should say so rather than inventing a memory.

Ideas from research

Memory as an operating system. MemGPT proposed virtual context management, borrowing from operating system memory hierarchies: the model pages information between a small, fast working context and larger external storage, using function calls to read, write and manage its own context1. The authors showed it maintaining consistency over long conversations and analysing documents larger than the context window1.

Retrieval by relevance, recency and importance. The Generative Agents paper gave simulated characters a memory stream of experiences, retrieved by combining how relevant, how recent and how important each memory is, plus periodic reflection that synthesises memories into higher-level conclusions2.

Indexing, retrieval and reading. LongMemEval's authors framed memory design as stages of indexing, retrieval and reading, and proposed improvements such as splitting sessions into smaller units, expanding memory keys with extracted facts, and making queries time-aware3.

Good memory isn't storing more. It's storing the right things in the right shape, and retrieving them with time and relevance in mind.

The memory architecture I use

LayerContentsLifetime
Working contextThe current task, recent turns, retrieved itemsOne request or session
Session summariesWhat was discussed, decided and left openWeeks to months
Profile and factsStable facts and preferences, each with source and timestampUntil changed or deleted
Episodic storePast interactions, indexed for retrievalDefined retention period
Organisational knowledgeDocuments and data the user may access, via RAGGoverned by the source system

Practical rules that make it work:

  1. Extract facts deliberately, as structured records with a source and timestamp, using structured outputs, rather than keeping raw transcripts as the only memory.
  2. Resolve conflicts by time. Newer facts supersede older ones; keep history but retrieve the current value.
  3. Retrieve with time awareness, so "last week's decision" finds last week's session.
  4. Let the model abstain. If retrieval finds nothing reliable, the answer is "I don't have that", not a guess.
  5. Evaluate memory specifically, with test cases for recall, updates and abstention, added to your agent evaluation suite.

Memory is personal data

A memory store is a profile of a person. Treat it accordingly:

  • Visibility and control. Users can see what is remembered, correct it and delete it.
  • Scope. Memory is partitioned per user and per tenant, with the same isolation tests as any multi-tenant store, as in multi-tenant SaaS patterns.
  • Sensitive categories. Don't store health, financial or other sensitive details without a clear basis and purpose, especially under regimes such as the UAE PDPL.
  • Retention. Define how long each layer is kept and enforce it automatically.
  • Injection risk. Content written into memory from untrusted sources can carry instructions into future sessions. Treat remembered content as data, with the controls in prompt injection defence.

Start small

Most products don't need the full stack on day one. A useful first version is session summaries plus a small, user-visible set of facts. Add episodic retrieval when evaluation shows users need it, and measure whether each layer improves outcomes enough to justify its cost and risk.

item.title: From HTI-1 to HTI-5: how US health IT certification rules for AI are shifting, and what to build anyway
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: HTI-1 set USCDI v3 and AI 'model card' duties for certified health IT; the HTI-5 proposal would remove many requirements, including those. What changed, and what to build regardless.
item.content:encoded:
In 2023 US health IT regulation added detailed transparency duties for AI in certified EHRs. Two years later, a deregulatory proposal would remove them. For health tech teams, the lesson is not to build only what the rule of the moment requires.

US health IT certification rules shape what millions of clinicians see in their EHRs. In late 2023 the HTI-1 final rule made the most significant AI-related changes yet: transparency duties for predictive decision support. In late 2025 the HTI-5 proposed rule set out to remove many certification requirements, including those AI duties. Health tech leaders are understandably asking what they actually need to build.

This is an architect's reading. Confirm the current status of each rule and how it applies to you with regulatory counsel.

What HTI-1 did

  • USCDI v3 as the baseline. HTI-1 adopted the United States Core Data for Interoperability version 3 as the baseline standard from 1 January 2026, replacing version 11.
  • Decision support interventions. It established a decision support interventions (DSI) criterion and added a predictive DSI category covering AI and machine learning capabilities2.
  • Source attributes. Developers supplying predictive DSIs as part of certified health IT had to make detailed source attribute information available for review, often described as model card requirements, with an enforcement date of 1 January 2025 for the DSI provisions2.

What HTI-5 proposes

In December 2025 ASTP/ONC published HTI-5, a deregulatory proposed rule. Commentary describes it as proposing to remove 34 and revise seven of the 60 certification criteria56. ASTP/ONC's own materials describe the DSI change as reducing the criterion's scope to remove the AI model card requirements34. Some changes were proposed to take effect on publication of a final rule and others later; sources differ on the details5.

Holland & Knight characterised the year-end actions as a strategic pivot in federal health IT policy6. Check whether HTI-5 has been finalised, and in what form, before changing plans.

Regulation can remove a requirement to publish model information. It can't remove a hospital's need to understand the model it is relying on.

Why I'd keep building transparency anyway

Whatever happens to the certification criterion, the underlying questions don't go away:

  • Customers ask. Health systems' AI governance committees often ask vendors what data a model was trained on, how it performs in different populations, and how it is monitored. A clear model description shortens procurement.
  • Other regimes apply. Products sold internationally may face the EU AI Act, and regulated device software may fall under FDA pathways such as those in FDA PCCPs.
  • Safety and liability. When a model contributes to a harmful outcome, the organisation that can show what it knew about the model, and how it monitored it, is in a far stronger position. See AI incident postmortems.
  • Policy swings. Requirements removed in one cycle can return in another. Building transparency as a product capability is cheaper than switching it on and off.

What I'd build regardless of the rule

  1. A model description per predictive feature: intended use, training data sources, known limitations, performance overall and by relevant subgroups, update history. Keep it as structured data, not a PDF.
  2. Local validation before go-live at each customer, because performance varies between sites; federation helps, as in federated health analytics.
  3. Ongoing monitoring for drift and subgroup performance, with a defined path for clinicians to report problems.
  4. Change control: every model update versioned, evaluated against a fixed set, and recorded.
  5. Interoperable data foundations: USCDI-aligned FHIR data, which most predictive features depend on, built with the patterns in FHIR Bulk Data pipelines and TEFCA.

These map neatly to general frameworks too, such as those compared in ISO 42001 and the NIST AI RMF, so one body of evidence serves several audiences.

For health systems

If you buy rather than build, don't let a relaxed certification requirement relax your procurement. Ask vendors for the same information HTI-1 described, contractually, and require notification of model changes. Your governance committee's questions shouldn't depend on which rule is in force this year.

item.title: The lakehouse catalog is your real lock-in: how to choose one in 2026
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Open table formats freed data files; the catalog now decides access, governance and portability. What Apache Polaris, Unity Catalog and the Iceberg REST API mean for your lakehouse.
item.content:encoded:
Open table formats like Iceberg promised that no vendor would own your data. They mostly delivered, for the files. But every engine still has to ask a catalog where tables are and who may read them, and that's where control has moved.

A few years ago the lakehouse argument was about table formats. That argument is largely settled: Apache Iceberg is widely supported, and I've covered its latest version in Apache Iceberg v3. The files sit in your own object storage in an open format any engine can read.

The quieter question is who every engine asks before reading those files. That is the catalog, and it has become the most strategic choice in a modern data platform.

Why the catalog holds the power

In an Iceberg lakehouse, the catalog tracks which tables exist, their current metadata and schema, and increasingly who may access them. Modern catalogs go further and issue engines short-lived storage credentials scoped to the tables they're allowed to read, a pattern called credential vending. Databricks' documentation, for example, describes Unity Catalog granting short-lived credentials to external systems that connect through its REST API or the Iceberg REST catalog interface, subject to explicit privileges and metastore settings4.

That is good security design. It also means the catalog is where permissions, lineage, audit and access for every engine live. Changing the catalog later is far harder than changing an engine.

Open files with a closed catalog is a more polite form of lock-in, but it's still lock-in. Evaluate catalogs as carefully as you once evaluated databases.

The open REST interface

The Iceberg REST catalog API is what makes multi-engine lakehouses practical: any engine that speaks it can work with any catalog that implements it. Apache Polaris is an open-source catalog built around that API, described by the Apache Software Foundation as a fully featured catalog for Iceberg that enables interoperability across engines such as Spark, Flink and Trino1.

Polaris entered the Apache incubator in 2024 after being donated by Snowflake and Dremio, and the foundation announced it as a top-level project in March 202612. Commentary on the graduation noted multiple releases and a broad contributor base2, and the 1.4 release added multi-tenancy and deployment improvements3. Top-level status means independent Apache governance, which matters if neutrality is part of why you chose an open catalog.

Unity Catalog takes a different route: a catalog with its own API that also exposes Iceberg REST access for external engines, alongside Delta support45. Check the current status of each capability, since some external access features have been labelled preview.

Questions I ask when choosing

QuestionWhy it matters
Which engines must read and write, today and in three years?Every engine needs a supported path through the catalog, including write access
Where are permissions defined, and can they be exported?Governance that can't leave the catalog is the deepest form of lock-in
Does it vend scoped, short-lived credentials?Avoids engines holding broad storage keys
Who governs the project or product?Foundation governance and vendor roadmaps carry different risks
Can it be self-hosted in-region?Residency rules, as in Saudi PDPL and UAE health data, may require it
How are lineage and audit exposed?Regulators and AI governance increasingly ask where data came from

Patterns that keep options open

  1. Standardise on the Iceberg REST interface for engine access, even if your catalog also offers proprietary APIs. That keeps engines swappable.
  2. Keep governance definitions as code: roles, grants and policies in version control, applied to the catalog, so they can be reapplied elsewhere.
  3. Use one catalog per governance domain, not one per engine. Several catalogs over the same tables invite inconsistency.
  4. Pair the catalog with data contracts, so table semantics and ownership travel with the data rather than living only in catalog metadata.
  5. Test an exit. Once a year, prove that a second engine, or a second catalog, can read critical tables. It's cheap insurance.

The AI angle

AI systems are now among the biggest consumers of lakehouse data: feature pipelines, training sets, retrieval indexes and agents querying tables directly. A catalog that vends scoped credentials and records access gives you one place to control what each AI workload may read, which supports the evidence expected in AI governance frameworks. Without it, every AI project tends to get its own copy of the data, and governance dissolves.

item.title: Securing the AI model supply chain: signing, provenance and safe formats
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Downloaded model weights can execute code and be tampered with. How pickle risks, model signing, SLSA provenance and ML bills of materials fit into a practical AI supply chain checklist.
item.content:encoded:
Teams that wouldn't run an unsigned binary from the internet routinely download model weights from public hubs and load them into production. Models are software artefacts, with software supply chain risks and a few of their own.

Software teams have spent a decade learning to verify what they run: signed packages, pinned dependencies, software bills of materials, reproducible builds. AI teams often skip all of it. A model is downloaded from a public hub by name, loaded with a single line of code and deployed. If that file had been tampered with, or was malicious from the start, few organisations would notice.

As more companies run open-weight models privately, as in private LLMs on-prem, this becomes a real attack surface.

The risks

Code execution on load. Hugging Face's own documentation warns that pickle, the default format for PyTorch weights, can enable arbitrary code execution when a file is loaded, and recommends safetensors as a safer alternative1. Security researchers have reported malicious models on public hubs that used this to plant backdoors, and noted that pickle isn't the only risky format: some Keras models can run code through Lambda layers2.

Scanners are imperfect. A 2026 study of malicious pickle-based models reported that existing scanners varied widely in how well they detected them on its dataset, which is a reason not to treat a scan as proof of safety7.

Tampering and substitution. Without signatures, there's no reliable way to know a model file is the one its publisher released, or that the copy in your registry hasn't changed since it was approved.

Unknown lineage. Fine-tuned models inherit everything about their base model and training data, including licence terms and possible poisoning. Without records, you can't answer basic questions in a security review or due diligence.

The building blocks

ControlWhat it gives you
Safe formatsWeights that load as data rather than executable code, such as safetensors1
Model signingVerification that a model is unchanged and from the expected publisher. The OpenSSF model-signing project released v1.0 in April 2025, built on Sigstore and supporting any model format and size34
Build provenanceA record of how an artefact was produced. SLSA's build track defines levels from provenance existing (L1), to signed provenance from a hosted build platform (L2), to a hardened build platform (L3)5
ML bill of materialsAn inventory of the model, datasets and dependencies. CycloneDX supports ML-BOMs and model cards for transparency into security, privacy, safety and ethical considerations6

Treat a model like a container image: pulled from a trusted registry, pinned by digest, verified on deployment, and traceable to how it was built.

The checklist

  1. Use an internal model registry. Production never pulls directly from public hubs. Models are imported, reviewed and stored internally.
  2. Prefer safe formats. Accept safetensors or equivalent where possible; convert or reject formats that execute code on load. Load untrusted files only in isolated sandboxes.
  3. Scan on import, while remembering scanners miss things. Scanning reduces risk; it doesn't certify safety.
  4. Pin by hash, not by name. Reference models by immutable digest so "latest" can never silently change what runs.
  5. Sign what you produce and verify what you run. Sign fine-tuned and approved models at the end of your pipeline, and verify signatures at deployment.
  6. Generate provenance in your training pipeline, aiming for at least signed provenance from a managed build platform, in the spirit of SLSA Build L2.
  7. Keep an ML-BOM per model: base model, datasets, licences, training configuration and evaluation results, linked to your AI system register.
  8. Restrict runtime permissions. Model-serving containers need no outbound internet access and minimal privileges, enforced with the policies in Kubernetes admission policies.
  9. Re-evaluate after every model change with your evaluation set, including safety and behaviour tests, not just accuracy.

Beyond the weights

The supply chain extends past model files. Datasets, tokenisers, prompt templates, agent tools and MCP servers all shape behaviour. MCP servers in particular deserve the same allow-listing and review, as covered in securing MCP servers. Google's announcement of model signing noted plans to extend the approach to datasets and other ML artefacts4, which is the right direction.

Why this matters now

Enterprise customers and regulators are starting to ask where models come from and how they are controlled. An ML-BOM, signed models and a registry answer those questions concretely, and support governance frameworks such as those compared in ISO 42001 and the NIST AI RMF. They are also inexpensive to adopt early and painful to retrofit after an incident.
