item.title: openEHR vs FHIR: why the best health platforms often use both
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: openEHR and FHIR are often framed as rivals. They solve different problems: governed clinical persistence and interoperable exchange. How they differ and how I combine them with OMOP.
item.content:encoded:
Ask a room of health informaticians whether to build on openEHR or FHIR and you will start a long argument. Most of it dissolves once you separate three jobs: storing clinical data well, exchanging it, and analysing it.

Health systems building a new clinical data platform, particularly in Europe, the Gulf and parts of Asia, often face this choice early. Vendors pitch one or the other. Standards communities defend their own. The decision gets framed as a winner-takes-all bet, when in practice the strongest platforms usually use each where it is strong.

Different jobs

A helpful way to see it, set out in one comparison of openEHR, FHIR and CDA, is as layers rather than rivals: FHIR for transactional exchange, openEHR for native persistence with clinical governance, and CDA for archival documents1.

openEHRFHIR
Primary jobLong-term, vendor-neutral clinical data persistenceExchanging data between systems via APIs5
Modelling approachTwo-level: stable reference model plus archetypes and templates2Resources, extended and constrained by profiles
Clinical governanceCommunity-reviewed archetypes in the Clinical Knowledge Manager6Implementation guides and profiles per programme or country
QueryingArchetype Query Language across the repositorySearch parameters; complex analytics usually done elsewhere
EcosystemStrong in parts of Europe, Australia and AsiaBroad global adoption and regulatory backing

What two-level modelling buys you

openEHR's central idea is separating the software model from clinical content. A stable reference model sits at the first level. Archetypes, each describing one clinical concept such as blood pressure, and templates, which combine and constrain archetypes for a specific use such as a discharge summary, sit at the second2. Clinicians can define and evolve content without the software changing underneath.

Archetypes are governed centrally and reused globally through the Clinical Knowledge Manager6. In community discussions, practitioners argue that archetypes express domain semantics independent of technology, while FHIR profiles tend to be scoped to particular implementations3. That's a perspective from the openEHR side, but the point about governance is fair: a well-reviewed archetype for blood pressure means the same thing in every system that uses it.

openEHR's real product is clinical agreement. The technology exists to keep that agreement stable while software and vendors change around it.

What FHIR does better

FHIR was built for exchange: resources, RESTful APIs and a web-developer-friendly approach5. It has become the default in regulation and procurement. US interoperability rules, prior authorisation APIs and bulk data access all build on it, as covered in CMS-0057-F and FHIR Bulk Data pipelines. Developers can be productive with FHIR quickly, and tools, libraries and test servers are plentiful.

Using a FHIR server as the primary store is where opinions diverge. One practitioner write-up argues it works for simpler cases but struggles with complex documents, temporal queries and archetype-level governance4. That is a vendor perspective; plenty of organisations do run FHIR-native repositories successfully. The question is how much clinical modelling depth and long-term governance you need.

The pattern I use: three layers

  1. Persistence. Where the organisation needs deep, governed clinical records over decades, an openEHR clinical data repository holds the source of truth, with templates agreed with clinicians.
  2. Exchange. FHIR APIs expose data to apps, partners, payers and national exchanges. A facade maps between openEHR compositions and FHIR resources, a pattern described in practice write-ups4.
  3. Analytics. An OMOP CDM, built downstream, serves research, quality and AI, with standard vocabularies as described in clinical terminologies and OMOP and the pipeline in FHIR to OMOP.

Where deep clinical modelling isn't needed, for example a digital health start-up with a narrow product, a FHIR-native store plus OMOP for analytics is often simpler and perfectly adequate.

How to decide

  • Who is the customer? National or regional health systems planning decades ahead lean towards openEHR for persistence. Products integrating with many partners lean towards FHIR first.
  • Who owns clinical content? If clinicians need to define and govern data models directly, openEHR's tooling is built for that.
  • What does regulation require? Exchange obligations almost always mean FHIR, whatever you store internally.
  • What skills can you hire? FHIR skills are more widely available; openEHR expertise is concentrated in particular regions and vendors.
  • What will you analyse? Neither is an analytics model. Plan for OMOP or a similar layer from the start.

Why it matters for AI

Clinical AI depends on data that means the same thing across sources and over time. Governed archetypes, consistent FHIR profiles and standard vocabularies all serve that goal. The worst foundation for AI is a mix of local models with no shared semantics, whatever standard name is on the label. That is an ontology problem first, and the same principles apply as in ontology, knowledge graph and semantic layer.

item.title: Inference gateways on Kubernetes: model-aware routing for self-hosted LLMs
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: LLM traffic breaks ordinary load balancing. How the Gateway API Inference Extension routes on live model-server metrics, what the benchmarks showed, and how I'd adopt it.
item.content:encoded:
Round-robin load balancing assumes requests are short and roughly equal. LLM requests are neither. The Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension adds model-aware routing to an ordinary gateway, and it changes how I design private model platforms.

When teams first put a self-hosted model behind Kubernetes, they usually reach for the familiar pattern: a Deployment of model servers, a Service in front, and a load balancer spreading requests evenly. It works in a demo. Under real load, some replicas sit with long queues and nearly full GPU memory while others are idle, and tail latency climbs even though the cluster as a whole has spare capacity.

Why LLM traffic breaks ordinary load balancing

The Kubernetes project's introduction to the Inference Extension puts it plainly: LLM inference sessions are often long-running, resource-intensive and partially stateful, and a single GPU-backed server may hold several sessions and in-memory token caches. Load balancers that route by HTTP path or round-robin don't account for model identity, request criticality or the current state of each server1.

Two requests to the same model can differ in cost by orders of magnitude, depending on prompt and output length. And as covered in LLM inference serving, sending a request to a replica that already holds its prompt prefix in cache is far cheaper than sending it anywhere else.

How the extension works

The Gateway API Inference Extension builds on Gateway API, keeping the familiar Gateway and HTTPRoute model and adding inference-specific steps15. Its central resource is the InferencePool: a pool of model-server pods on shared compute, similar to a Service but aware of model serving1. The project documentation lists InferencePool as generally available since v1.0.02.

The original design separated responsibilities by persona: platform operators manage where and how models are served through pools, while model owners manage what is served, including traffic splitting between versions1. The model-facing APIs have continued to evolve, so check the current documentation for your version.

The request flow

A request reaches the gateway, which matches an HTTPRoute to an InferencePool. Instead of forwarding to any pod, the gateway consults an endpoint selection extension, often called the endpoint picker, which examines live pod metrics such as queue length, memory use and loaded adapters, and chooses the pod that can serve the request most efficiently1. Gateway implementations describe the picker tracking signals such as KV-cache utilisation and queue length4.

To the client it's still one ordinary request. The intelligence lives in the gateway layer, where the platform team controls it.

What the benchmark showed

The project compared the extension with a standard Kubernetes Service for a vLLM deployment on H100 GPUs, ramping traffic from 100 to 1,000 queries per second. Throughput was roughly on par, but the extension showed significantly lower p90 per-output-token latency at higher load, and lower end-to-end tail latency as traffic rose beyond about 400 to 500 queries per second1. The authors attribute this to avoiding hotspots that ordinary load balancing creates for long-running inference requests1.

Tail latency is what users feel, and GPU hotspots are what finance pays for. Model-aware routing improves both without buying another GPU.

How I'd adopt it

  1. Start from Gateway API. If your clusters still use an Ingress controller, the move to Gateway API is the prerequisite and has its own value.
  2. Pick a gateway implementation that supports the Inference Extension, and confirm which version of the APIs it implements.
  3. Expose metrics from your model servers that the endpoint picker needs, and check them under load before trusting the routing.
  4. Load test against your own traffic, comparing tail latency and cost per request with your current setup, as in LLM inference serving.
  5. Use pools to separate concerns: interactive and batch traffic, regulated and general workloads, or different hardware classes.
  6. Combine with scheduling and cost controls: GPU allocation through DRA, training jobs through gang scheduling, and spend visibility through FOCUS-based cost allocation.

Where it fits in a private AI platform

An inference gateway is the routing layer in the platform described in private LLMs on-prem and where to run models in the UAE. Above it sits the policy gateway that handles authentication, model approval and logging; below it, the serving engines and GPUs. Keeping those layers distinct makes each easier to change.

item.title: Structured outputs: how to make LLMs dependable components of real systems
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Schema-constrained outputs make LLM responses machine-readable by design, but can hurt reasoning if used carelessly. How structured outputs work and how I design LLM integrations with them.
item.content:encoded:
Most enterprise value from LLMs comes when their output feeds another system: a database, a workflow, an API. That needs data in a known shape, every time. Structured outputs solve the format problem. They don't solve the correctness problem, and used carelessly they can make it worse.

The first version of most LLM integrations parses free text. Someone writes a prompt asking for JSON, adds a regular expression to extract it, and a retry loop for when it fails. It works in testing. In production, a small percentage of responses arrive with a trailing comment, a missing bracket or a field renamed on a whim, and the pipeline breaks at three in the morning.

Structured outputs remove that class of failure. They're one of the most useful features model providers have shipped for enterprise integration. But they are often treated as a correctness guarantee, which they aren't.

What structured outputs are

You supply a JSON schema, and the provider constrains generation so the response must match it. OpenAI introduced Structured Outputs in August 2024, available through strict function definitions and a JSON schema response format, and reported that its model at the time achieved 100% schema adherence in its own evaluations1. The approach restricts which tokens the model may produce at each step to those consistent with the schema, building on techniques from open-source constrained generation tools2.

Anthropic's documentation describes two related features: JSON outputs that shape the response, and strict tool use that enforces schema compliance on tool inputs through grammar-constrained sampling34. Both providers document limits on which JSON Schema features are supported, and output can still be incomplete if generation stops early, for example at a token limit13.

Structured outputs guarantee shape, not truth. A perfectly valid object with the wrong invoice total is still wrong; it's just wrong in a format your system will happily accept.

The reasoning trade-off

Constraining format has a cost. In "Let Me Speak Freely?", presented at EMNLP 2024, researchers compared constrained decoding, format instructions in the prompt, and generating free text first then converting it. They found that strict format restrictions such as JSON mode were associated with a significant decline in reasoning performance, with stricter constraints generally doing more harm. On classification tasks, though, strict formats could help by reducing answer selection errors5.

The practical lesson is to separate thinking from formatting:

  • For extraction and classification, strict schemas are usually a clear win.
  • For tasks that need reasoning, give the model room to reason first, either in a free-text field within the schema placed before the answer fields, or in a separate step, then produce the structured result. The paper also found that simple corrective steps, such as reformatting outputs that fail to parse, improve reliability5.
  • Measure both ways on your own evaluation set before standardising.

Designing schemas that help the model

  1. Keep schemas small and flat where possible. Deeply nested, highly optional schemas are harder for models and may hit provider complexity limits.
  2. Use enums for categories instead of free strings, so downstream systems never see an unexpected label.
  3. Make uncertainty representable. Include an explicit "unknown" or "not found" option and a place for a short reason, so the model isn't forced to invent a value to satisfy a required field.
  4. Describe fields clearly. Field descriptions are part of the prompt; vague names produce vague values.
  5. Order fields deliberately. Put evidence or reasoning fields before conclusions, so the model generates support before the answer.
  6. Version schemas like any interface, with the contract discipline in data contracts.

Validate the content, not just the shape

Once format failures disappear, the remaining failures are about meaning. The checks I put after every structured call:

  • Business rules in code: totals add up, dates are in range, referenced IDs exist, a refund doesn't exceed the order value.
  • Cross-checks against source: extracted values that should appear in the input document actually do.
  • Confidence routing: low-confidence or "unknown" results go to a person instead of straight into the system of record.
  • Evaluation on real cases, field by field, as in evaluation sets that predict production. Report accuracy per field, not just "valid JSON rate".

Structured outputs and agents

For agents, strict tool definitions mean every tool call arrives with well-formed arguments, which removes a whole category of runtime errors. It doesn't make those calls safe. Arguments still need authorisation and policy checks outside the model, and the session-level containment described in prompt injection defence and MCP tool annotations. A schema-valid instruction to transfer money to the wrong account is still the wrong instruction.

A note on portability

Providers implement structured outputs differently, with different parameters and supported schema subsets. If you use several models, as in model routing, keep one canonical schema in your codebase and let a gateway translate it per provider, then test each route. Self-hosted models can get similar behaviour from constrained decoding in the serving layer, covered in LLM inference serving.

item.title: OpenTelemetry goes 'stable by default': what it means for Kubernetes telemetry, and how to migrate
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: OpenTelemetry is prioritising stability, and the Kubernetes attributes processor hit v1.0.0 with stable conventions and breaking renames. What changed and how I'd plan the migration.
item.content:encoded:
OpenTelemetry has spent its first years growing fast. Its governance committee has now made stability the priority, and the first big results are landing in Kubernetes telemetry, including attribute renames that will touch dashboards and alerts.

Ask platform teams what frustrates them about OpenTelemetry and stability comes up quickly: components at different maturity levels, attribute names that change between releases, and upgrades that quietly break dashboards. The project has heard the same thing. In November 2025 its Governance Committee wrote that complexity and lack of stability were creating impediments to production deployments, and set out a plan to change priorities1.

A year on, the first concrete results are in, and Kubernetes telemetry is where most platform teams will feel them.

What 'stable by default' means

The committee's goals were explicit1:

  • All OpenTelemetry distributions should be stable by default, with standard mechanisms to opt in to experimental features.
  • A single, consistent set of stability criteria, including documentation, performance testing and benchmarks.
  • Easier stabilisation of instrumentation libraries, and federation of semantic conventions.
  • Epoch releases that are easier for organisations to consume.

For a platform team, the practical promise is fewer surprises: stable components you can rely on, and clearly marked opt-ins for anything that isn't.

The Kubernetes example

The Kubernetes attributes processor, which enriches telemetry with metadata such as pod, namespace and node, shows what that journey involves. Its stability depended on the Kubernetes semantic conventions it emits, so the two efforts moved together23:

WhenWhat happened
Nov 2025The Kubernetes semantic conventions group began focused work on stabilising Kubernetes attributes, in step with the Collector's stability goals2
Mar 2026Kubernetes attributes reached release candidate; the processor offered feature gates to try the new schema2
Jun 2026The attributes shipped as stable in Semantic Conventions v1.42.034
Sep 2026The Kubernetes attributes processor reached v1.0.0, meeting the Collector's stable criteria3

The v1.0.0 announcement is clear that moving to the new convention names means some breakage for existing users, and points to a migration guide35. During the transition the processor provided feature gates, processor.k8sattributes.EmitV1K8sConventions and processor.k8sattributes.DontEmitV0K8sConventions, so teams could emit the new attributes before dropping the old ones2.

Stability is a one-time cost paid up front: a final round of renames, then a long period where names stop moving. It's worth paying deliberately rather than discovering it in a broken dashboard.

Why attribute renames hurt more than they look

Kubernetes attributes are everywhere in an observability estate: dashboard filters, alert rules, service level objectives, cost allocation by namespace, retention policies, access controls and the queries engineers keep in runbooks. A renamed attribute doesn't throw an error. It just makes a filter match nothing, so a dashboard goes quiet and an alert never fires.

The migration plan I use

  1. Inventory dependencies on attribute names. Export dashboards, alert rules, recording rules and saved queries, and search them for the Kubernetes attributes in your telemetry. Include cost reports that group by namespace or workload, as in Kubernetes FinOps.
  2. Read the migration guide for your exact version of the Collector and processor5, and list old and new names side by side.
  3. Emit both, then switch. Where your version supports it, emit the new conventions alongside the old in a non-production environment, update dashboards and alerts to the new names, then stop emitting the old ones.
  4. Use the gateway layer to manage the transition centrally rather than on every node, which is one reason I favour the agent-to-gateway pattern in Collector deployment patterns.
  5. Add canary checks: alerts that fire when a key dashboard query returns no data, so silent breakage is caught.
  6. Pin Collector versions and upgrade deliberately, with a changelog review for every component you use.

A broader stability strategy

The Kubernetes processor is one component among many working towards stability3. The same pattern applies elsewhere, from the span events deprecation to GenAI conventions that are still evolving, covered in LLM observability. My rules for platform teams:

  • Prefer stable components in production, and record each experimental component you depend on with the reason and an owner.
  • Treat telemetry schemas as interfaces, with the same versioning discipline as APIs and the contract thinking in data contracts.
  • Budget a small, regular amount of time for observability upgrades, rather than a painful catch-up every two years.

item.title: Technical due diligence for AI companies: the checklist I use for investors and acquirers
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: AI start-ups fail diligence in new ways: no evaluations, borrowed moats, uncontained agents, unclear data rights. The checklist I use when assessing an AI company for investors or acquirers.
item.content:encoded:
Classic technical due diligence asks whether the software is well built and the team can scale it. For AI companies those questions still matter, but a new set sits on top: is the AI actually good, is it defensible, is it safe, and does the company have the right to the data behind it?

A typical AI pitch deck shows a polished demo, impressive early revenue and a slide titled "proprietary AI". Diligence is where that slide meets reality. The traditional checklist (code quality, architecture, security, team, scalability) still applies. But AI companies add risks that a conventional review can miss entirely, and some of them go straight to valuation.

This is the checklist I work through when assessing an AI company for an investor or acquirer. It's organised as questions, with the evidence I'd expect to see.

1. Does the AI actually work, and how do they know?

  • Is there a maintained evaluation set? Real examples, labelled with expected outcomes, run on every model or prompt change. If quality is judged by demos and anecdotes, that's the single biggest red flag. I describe what good looks like in evaluation sets that predict production.
  • Is reliability measured, not just average accuracy? For agents, a single success rate hides inconsistency. Research on τ-bench introduced pass^k, the chance of succeeding on every one of k attempts, and found that agents were notably less consistent than their single-run success rates suggested5. See evaluating AI agents.
  • Is there production monitoring? Feedback, escalations, sampled reviews and drift checks, tied to the evaluation set.
  • Can they show improvement over time, with numbers from the same evaluation set across releases?

2. What is actually defensible?

  • Which parts are theirs? Separate the third-party model, open-source components and the company's own work: data pipelines, evaluation, domain logic, workflow integration, proprietary data.
  • What happens when the underlying model improves? If a better general model would make the product unnecessary, the moat is thin. If better models make the product better, that's healthier.
  • Is there a data advantage? Proprietary data, feedback loops from usage, or curated domain knowledge such as a governed ontology or knowledge graph are harder to copy than prompts.
  • How portable are they across model providers? A gateway and evaluation set that let them switch models are both a risk control and a negotiating position. See build vs buy for AI.

"We fine-tuned a model" is not a moat by itself. A moat is something a well-funded competitor couldn't reproduce in a quarter with the same public models.

3. Do they have the right to their data?

  • Provenance. Where did training, fine-tuning and retrieval data come from, under what licence or agreement?
  • Customer data use. Do contracts allow customer data to be used for training or evaluation? Is that used in practice, and is it consistent with the contract?
  • Personal and sensitive data. How is personal, health or financial data handled in prompts, logs, embeddings and evaluation sets? Residency matters for some markets, as in UAE health data and Saudi PDPL.
  • Deletion. Can they actually delete a customer's data from every store, including vector indexes and caches?

4. Is the AI secure and contained?

  • Known risk categories. Has the team assessed the product against a recognised list such as the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications1?
  • Prompt injection. The UK NCSC has argued that prompt injection may never be fully mitigated the way SQL injection was6, so the question is containment: what can a compromised agent actually do? See prompt injection defence.
  • Tool and data permissions. Are agent tools scoped per user, enforced outside the model, and logged? See securing MCP servers.
  • Tenant isolation. Can retrieval ever return another customer's data? Ask for the test that proves it can't.

5. Is the engineering organisation healthy?

  • Delivery metrics. Deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and recovery time, with trends. DORA's 2025 research found that AI tends to amplify an organisation's existing strengths and weaknesses4, so a team leaning heavily on AI coding tools without good foundations may be accumulating risk; see DORA metrics in the AI era.
  • Key-person risk. Is the AI capability concentrated in one or two people? What's documented?
  • Decision records. Are major architecture choices written down, as in architecture decision records?

6. Do the unit economics hold?

  • Cost per outcome. Model, infrastructure and human review cost per resolved ticket, document or transaction, not just per token.
  • Sensitivity. What happens to margins if usage grows ten times, or a provider changes pricing?
  • Levers in use. Caching, routing and right-sized models, as in prompt caching and model routing. Unused levers are upside; no visibility at all is a risk.

7. What is the regulatory exposure?

  • Classification. Could any use case fall into a regulated or high-risk category under the EU AI Act3, or sector rules in health, finance or employment?
  • Governance evidence. An AI system register, risk assessments, incident handling and training. Frameworks such as the NIST AI RMF2 are a reasonable yardstick; see ISO 42001 or NIST AI RMF.
  • Customer commitments. What have they promised enterprise customers about AI, and can they evidence it?

Reading the results

No early-stage company will score well on everything, and that's not the point. Diligence should separate fixable gaps, such as missing monitoring or undocumented decisions, from structural problems, such as no data rights, no evaluation discipline or a product that a better general model would replace. The first belong in a post-investment plan with owners and dates. The second belong in the valuation conversation.

item.title: Prompt caching: the cheapest LLM cost and latency win most teams leave on the table
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Prompt caching can cut cost and latency on repeated prompt prefixes, but only if prompts are designed for it. How caching works across major providers and how I structure prompts for it.
item.content:encoded:
Most production prompts repeat the same long prefix on every call: system instructions, policies, tool definitions, reference documents. Every major model provider now offers a way to stop paying full price for it. Whether you benefit depends almost entirely on how your prompts are built.

Look at the prompts your AI product actually sends. In many production systems, the first several thousand tokens are identical on every call: the system prompt, safety and style rules, tool definitions, perhaps a policy document or schema. Only the last few hundred tokens are specific to the user and the request. Yet many teams pay full input price, and wait for full processing, on that repeated prefix every time.

Prompt caching exists to fix exactly that. It is usually the cheapest optimisation available, and the most commonly wasted.

How it works

When a model processes a prompt, it builds internal state for every token. If the next request begins with exactly the same tokens, that work can in principle be reused rather than repeated. Self-hosted serving engines do this with prefix caching on top of memory management techniques such as PagedAttention5, which I cover in LLM inference serving. Hosted model providers expose the same idea as a pricing and latency feature.

The key word is prefix. Caches match from the start of the prompt. Change one token near the beginning and everything after it is a miss.

How the major providers differ

ProviderHow it's enabledWhat the documentation describes
Anthropic (Claude)Explicit cache breakpoints in the requestA default cache lifetime of five minutes, refreshed on use, with a one-hour option; cache writes cost more than base input and cache reads cost a small fraction of it14
OpenAIAutomatic for long enough promptsApplies automatically to prompts of 1,024 tokens or more, with hits in 128-token increments and cached tokens reported in the usage data2
Google GeminiImplicit by default on recent models, or explicit cachesImplicit caching passes savings through on hits without a guarantee; explicit caching lets you create a cache with a configurable time to live3

Prices, minimum sizes and lifetimes change, and differ by model and by cloud platform. Read the current documentation for the models you actually use, and measure, rather than relying on any table, including this one.

Explicit caching rewards teams who design for it. Automatic caching rewards teams who happen to have stable prefixes. Either way, prompt structure decides the outcome.

Why most teams miss

The usual culprits are small and easy to fix once you look:

  • A timestamp or request ID at the top of the system prompt, so every prefix is unique.
  • The user's name or account details injected into the system prompt rather than the user turn.
  • Tool definitions in a different order on each request, because they're built from an unordered map.
  • Retrieved documents placed before the static instructions.
  • Prompt templates edited constantly, invalidating caches across all traffic with every deployment.
  • Traffic too sparse for the cache lifetime: if a given prefix is used once an hour and the cache lasts minutes, it will rarely hit.

The playbook

  1. Order prompts from most stable to least stable. Static instructions and tool definitions first, then slowly changing reference material, then per-user context, then the request itself.
  2. Make serialisation deterministic. Sort tool definitions and keys, fix whitespace and formatting, and version templates so the same version always produces the same bytes.
  3. Move volatile values to the end. Dates, user details and request metadata belong in the final turn, not the system prompt.
  4. Use explicit breakpoints where available, placing them after the large stable sections. Consider the longer lifetime for traffic that is regular but not constant, and compare the extra write cost with the expected reads1.
  5. Measure hit rates from usage data. Providers report cached tokens in responses123. Record them per route in your gateway alongside cost, as in FOCUS and AI spend.
  6. Treat prompt changes as cache events. A template change resets caching for that route. Batch changes and watch cost after deployment.
  7. Route consistently. If you use several models or regions, send requests with the same prefix to the same destination where possible, so caches have a chance to warm. The same logic applies to replicas in self-hosted serving.

Where it pays most

  • Agents. Long system prompts and large tool catalogues, repeated across many steps of the same task. Caching often makes multi-step agents economically viable; see evaluating AI agents for keeping them reliable too.
  • Document question answering. When users ask several questions about the same long document, cache the document once and vary the question, which pairs well with the approach in long context or RAG.
  • Batch processing with a shared instruction block and many short inputs.
  • Coding assistants that resend large amounts of repository context on each turn.

It pays least for short prompts, highly personalised prompts and very low traffic, where little is shared or the cache expires between uses.

Caching, routing and the gateway

Prompt caching interacts with the other cost levers. Model routing that sends similar requests to different models can split traffic and lower hit rates on each. Retrieval that returns results in a different order each time defeats caching of the retrieved section. A gateway that owns prompt assembly, routing and measurement in one place is the simplest way to manage these trade-offs, and it's the same gateway that enforces security policies in securing MCP servers.

Data protection note

Caching keeps processed prompt state on the provider's side for a period. For regulated data, check each provider's documentation and your agreements on how cached content is isolated and retained, and whether that is compatible with obligations such as those in the HIPAA Security Rule proposal or Gulf residency rules. For the most sensitive workloads, self-hosted serving with prefix caching keeps the cache inside your own boundary.

item.title: Federated health analytics: how to generate evidence without moving patient data
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: OHDSI network studies run the same analysis at many sites and share only aggregates. How federated health analytics works, where it's heading in Europe and the Gulf, and how I design it.
item.content:encoded:
Health data is increasingly required to stay where it is: inside a hospital, a country or a secure environment. Federated analytics turns that from a blocker into a design principle. The OHDSI network has been doing it at scale for years, and its lessons apply well beyond research.

The traditional way to answer a question across many hospitals was to copy their data into one place. That approach is getting harder every year. Data protection law, health-specific localisation rules, hospital governance and plain institutional caution all push the same way: the data stays where it is.

Federated analytics flips the model. Instead of bringing data to the analysis, you send the analysis to the data, run it locally at each site, and combine only the results.

How OHDSI does it

The OHDSI community is one of the largest working examples. The Book of OHDSI describes a network of more than 100 databases standardised to the OMOP CDM, collectively representing over a billion patient records at the time of writing1. A study becomes a network study when it runs across multiple CDMs at different institutions1.

The rules are strict and simple. Each site runs the same study package against its own CDM. A local analyst reviews the outputs before anything leaves, and minimum cell counts suppress small numbers. Only aggregate results such as summary statistics, estimates and diagnostics are shared. In the book's words, OHDSI network studies do not share patient-level data, and patient-level data from different sites is never pooled centrally1.

Why it works: standardise first

Federation only works if the same code means the same thing everywhere. That is why OHDSI insists on the CDM and its standardised vocabularies. The book is explicit about the design shift this requires: you are building a study package to run at sites whose data you will never see, so concept sets must be exhaustive rather than tuned to your own data, and code must be parameterised for different database platforms1.

The same discipline shows up in cohort definitions: definitions are portable, versioned artefacts, not local SQL.

Federation moves the hard work from data transfer agreements to data standardisation. That's a better trade: standardisation compounds, while every transfer agreement starts from zero.

The operational reality

The book is candid that network studies take real coordination. Site start-up can involve ethics approvals, database permissions, configuring an analysis environment, reviewing study code and getting dependencies installed within local IT constraints1. Data quality varies between sites, and study leads may review quality reports or run checks to understand variation1. It also notes that much of the process has been manual, with the community working to systematise it1.

In practice, the technical parts are rarely what slows a network down. Governance, trust and site capacity are. Architecture can help by making each site's job as small and predictable as possible.

Where regulation is heading

Europe. The European Health Data Space regulation, Regulation (EU) 2025/327, was published in March 2025 and sets up a framework for secondary use of health data for purposes such as research, innovation and public health3. Commentary notes that secondary use of personal electronic health data is to take place within secure processing environments, with health data access bodies handling permits34. Check the regulation for application dates, which are phased.

The Gulf. The UAE's health data law restricts storing and processing health data outside the country unless an exception applies, with research among the circumstances commentary describes5; I cover the detail in UAE health data localisation. Saudi Arabia's transfer rules add their own conditions, as in Saudi PDPL and cross-border AI.

Different regimes, same direction: analysis has to go to the data, or to a controlled environment, rather than data going wherever analysts happen to be.

The architecture I use

  1. A standard node. Each site gets the same deployable stack: an OMOP CDM, vocabularies, data quality tooling as in OMOP data quality checks, and an analysis runtime. Infrastructure as code makes new sites predictable.
  2. Signed, reviewed study packages. Analyses arrive as versioned packages, reviewed and approved before they run, never as ad hoc queries.
  3. Output controls at the edge. Minimum cell counts, automated disclosure checks and a human review step before results leave the site.
  4. A coordination layer that never sees patient data: study registry, package distribution, results collection and audit trail.
  5. Monitoring of the network itself: which sites are current on CDM and vocabulary versions, data quality status, and study participation.

And AI?

Federated approaches extend to model development: training or evaluating models site by site and sharing parameters or metrics rather than data. The same principles apply, with more care, because model outputs can leak information in ways summary statistics usually don't. At minimum, I'd use federation for external validation: testing a model built at one site against many others before anyone claims it generalises. That is where a lot of clinical AI falls short, and a network makes it routine.

item.title: Long context or RAG? What the research says about very large context windows
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Million-token context windows tempt teams to skip retrieval. Research on lost-in-the-middle, RULER and context rot shows why that's risky, and how I combine long context with RAG.
item.content:encoded:
Context windows have grown from a few thousand tokens to hundreds of thousands and more. It's tempting to stop building retrieval and just put everything in the prompt. The research suggests that bigger windows change the trade-offs, but don't remove them.

Every few months a model ships with a bigger context window, and the same question comes up: do we still need retrieval? If the model can read the whole policy manual, the full contract set or a year of support tickets in one go, why maintain chunking, embeddings, indexes and ranking at all?

It's a fair question, and for some workloads the answer really is "less than before". But the research on how models use long inputs is consistent enough that I don't treat a large window as a substitute for deciding what the model should read.

Three findings worth knowing

Position matters. In "Lost in the Middle", Liu and colleagues studied how models use long inputs in tasks such as multi-document question answering. Performance was often highest when the relevant information appeared at the beginning or end of the context and dropped when it was in the middle1. A later survey of long-context modelling describes this as a U-shaped curve5. The practical implication: where a fact sits in a long prompt can change whether it's used.

Advertised windows overstate useful windows. NVIDIA's RULER benchmark extended simple needle-in-a-haystack tests with harder tasks such as multi-hop tracing and aggregation. Models that scored almost perfectly on the simple test showed large drops as context length grew, and the authors report that many models fell below their quality threshold well before reaching their claimed context lengths2. Finding one sentence in a haystack is a much easier job than reasoning across a long document.

Longer inputs degrade reliability. Chroma's 2025 "Context Rot" report tested 18 models, including several frontier models, on deliberately simple tasks, keeping difficulty constant while increasing input length. Performance grew increasingly unreliable as input grew, and models didn't use their context uniformly3. The authors note that real tasks are more complex, so the effect may be larger in practice, and they published their code for replication34.

A model that can accept a million tokens has not promised to use all of them equally well. Capacity and attention are different things.

The other costs of stuffing the context

Quality isn't the only issue. Every token in the prompt costs money and adds latency on every request, unless the same prefix is cached and reused, which I cover in LLM inference serving. Long prompts are also harder to debug: when an answer is wrong, it is much harder to tell which of 200 pages misled the model than which of five retrieved passages did.

There's a governance cost too. Retrieval enforces access control naturally: you only fetch documents the user is allowed to see. "Put everything in the prompt" either ignores permissions or rebuilds them in a less tested way. For regulated data, that alone usually settles the question, as discussed in the HIPAA Security Rule proposal and UAE health data localisation.

When long context genuinely helps

None of this means long context is a gimmick. It changes what good retrieval looks like:

  • Bigger, more coherent chunks. Instead of 300-token fragments, retrieve whole sections or whole documents, so the model sees definitions and exceptions alongside the rule.
  • Single-document deep work. Reviewing one contract, one codebase module or one patient record against a checklist is a good fit, especially with the most important material placed at the start or end.
  • Fewer retrieval misses. A wider net for recall, followed by a model that reads more candidates, can beat aggressive filtering that drops the right passage.
  • Stable reference material. Long, unchanging context such as a policy manual or schema can be cached as a prefix and reused across requests.

How I design it: retrieve, then read generously

WorkloadApproach
Questions over a large, changing corpusRAG with larger chunks and reranking; long context only for the top results
Analysis of one long documentLong context, with key instructions and questions at the start and end
Whole-corpus themes and patternsNeither alone; consider GraphRAG or map-reduce summarisation
Facts about known entitiesQuery a governed knowledge graph, then explain with the model
Agents working over many stepsKeep working context small; summarise and store state rather than accumulating everything

The common thread is what is now called context engineering: deciding deliberately what goes into the window, in what order, and what stays out. Retrieval, ranking, summarisation and memory are all tools for that decision. A large window gives you more room to be generous; it doesn't remove the need to choose.

Test it on your own data

Published benchmarks tell you the direction of the effect, not its size for your documents. Before choosing an approach, I run a simple comparison on the client's own evaluation set, as described in evaluation sets that predict production:

  1. Baseline RAG with the current chunking and top-k.
  2. RAG with larger chunks and more results, using the long window to read more.
  3. Full-document long context for the subset of questions where it is feasible.
  4. Position tests: the same answer-bearing passage placed at the start, middle and end of the context.

Measure accuracy, citation correctness, latency and cost per answer for each. The result is usually a hybrid, and the numbers make the case to stakeholders far better than any article, including this one.

The bottom line

Bigger context windows are a genuine improvement. They make retrieval more forgiving, enable new single-document workflows and reduce some engineering effort. But the evidence on position effects, effective context length and degradation with input size means the most reliable systems still choose what the model reads. Treat the window as a budget to spend well, not a bucket to fill.

item.title: ISO/IEC 42001 or the NIST AI RMF? How to choose, and how to use both
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: NIST's AI RMF is a voluntary method; ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management system. How they differ, how they fit together, and how I'd sequence them for an AI company.
item.content:encoded:
Enterprise buyers increasingly ask AI vendors how they govern their AI. Two frameworks come up most: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001. They solve different problems, and most companies will end up using both.

The security questionnaire used to ask about SOC 2. Now it often has a section on AI: how do you identify AI risks, who approves new models, how do you monitor them? Two frameworks dominate the answers, and they are often presented as alternatives. They aren't.

Two different kinds of thing

NIST AI RMFISO/IEC 42001
What it isA voluntary framework for managing AI riskA standard for an AI management system
StructureFour functions: govern, map, measure, manage1Management system clauses plus AI-specific controls2
CertificationNone; you use itCertifiable by accredited bodies
StrengthPractical risk thinking across the AI lifecycleRepeatable governance with audit and continual improvement
Typical audienceInternal teams, US government and buyersEnterprise customers and international markets wanting assurance

A common way to put it: the NIST framework is something you use, while ISO/IEC 42001 is something you certify against4. Commentators note that ISO's management-system elements, such as internal audit, management review and continual improvement, have no direct equivalent in the NIST framework3.

They map onto each other

NIST's AI Resource Center hosts a crosswalk between the AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001. Commentators point out that it was contributed by the community rather than written by NIST, and that inclusion doesn't imply endorsement35. Informally, the four NIST functions line up with ISO's leadership and policy, context and impact assessment, monitoring, and review and improvement activities3. Treat such mappings as starting points rather than proof of coverage.

Use NIST to decide what to do about AI risk. Use ISO/IEC 42001 to prove you do it consistently. They answer different questions.

How I'd sequence them

  1. Start with an AI system register. Every framework, and every regulation, begins with knowing which AI systems you have, what they do and who owns them.
  2. Apply the NIST functions to your highest-risk systems first. Map context and impacts, measure with real evaluations, manage with controls and incident response.
  3. Build the evidence as you go: evaluation results, approval records, incident postmortems, training records. These are what auditors and customers ask for.
  4. Add the management system when customers or markets ask for certification: policy, roles, internal audit, management review.
  5. Map once to many. The same controls support the EU AI Act, SOC 2 and Gulf regimes such as DIFC Regulation 10.

Where engineering carries the load

Frameworks fail when they live only in documents. The controls that hold up in an audit are the ones built into systems: a model gateway that enforces approved models and logs every call, evaluation pipelines that gate releases as in evaluating AI agents, incident handling as in AI incident postmortems, and role-based training as in AI literacy. Build those and the paperwork follows; write the paperwork alone and it drifts from reality within months.

item.title: OpenTelemetry is deprecating the Span Events API: what to change, and when
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: OpenTelemetry is moving events from span events to log-based events. What the deprecation means for instrumentation, dashboards and AI telemetry, and how I'd prepare.
item.content:encoded:
For years there were two ways to record an event in OpenTelemetry. The project has chosen one: events are logs with names, correlated with traces. Existing data keeps working, but new instrumentation should change direction.

If you have instrumented code with OpenTelemetry, you have probably called Span.AddEvent or Span.RecordException. In March 2026 the project announced it is deprecating that API. New events should be emitted as logs, correlated with the active span through context1.

It sounds like a small API change. For platform teams it touches instrumentation guidelines, dashboards, cost and, increasingly, AI telemetry.

Why the change

OpenTelemetry has offered two ways to emit events correlated with traces: span events via the Tracing API, and log-based events via the Logs API134. The announcement lists the problems with having both: split guidance for library authors, duplicate concepts for operators, and slower evolution because every improvement had to be specified twice1. The community has converged on a simpler model: events are logs with names, emitted via the Logs API and correlated through context, a direction set out in an earlier post on logging12.

What changes and what doesn't

ChangingStaying the same
Span event APIs such as AddEvent and RecordException are deprecated in the tracing specificationExisting span event data remains valid in the OTLP trace model
SDKs make log-based events first-classCorrelation across signals works the same way
Instrumentations and semantic conventions move to log-based events in their next major versionsCompatibility options can still show events on spans

As the authors put it, they are deprecating the API for recording span events, not the ability to see events attached to spans1.

The practical risk isn't broken code. It's a dashboard or alert that quietly stops showing exceptions because they now arrive as logs instead of span events.

What I'd do now

  1. Update instrumentation guidelines. New code emits events and exceptions as log-based events correlated with the current span.
  2. Check the logs pipeline. If logs aren't collected through OpenTelemetry yet, events will have nowhere to go. A Collector gateway, as in Collector deployment patterns, is the natural place to route them.
  3. Audit dashboards and alerts that depend on span events, especially exception counts and error views, and test them after each instrumentation upgrade, as the project recommends1.
  4. Confirm backend support for showing log-based events in trace views, so engineers don't lose context when debugging.
  5. Watch costs. Moving events to the logs pipeline may change how they are priced and retained by your vendor. Model it before the switch.

Why this matters for AI telemetry

AI applications produce a lot of event-like data: prompts, responses, tool calls, guardrail decisions. Treating these as named, structured log events correlated with traces fits the GenAI observability work described in LLM observability with OpenTelemetry. It also makes it easier to apply separate retention, redaction and access rules to sensitive content than when it is embedded in spans.

item.title: Clinical terminologies explained: SNOMED, LOINC, RxNorm and the OMOP vocabularies
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Healthcare data speaks many coding systems. How SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm and ICD relate, how the OMOP Standardized Vocabularies unify them, and why this matters for health AI.
item.content:encoded:
The same diagnosis can arrive as an ICD code, a SNOMED concept, a Read code or free text. Any serious health data or AI platform has to reconcile them. The OMOP Standardized Vocabularies are one of the most practical ways to do it.

Healthcare has never had a single language. Hospitals bill in one coding system, record diagnoses in another, report lab results in a third and prescribe in a fourth. Countries add their own variants. Anyone building analytics, research or AI on health data meets this problem in the first week, and it is fundamentally an ontology problem.

The main terminologies

TerminologyUsed mainly forTypical role in analytics
SNOMED CTClinical findings, conditions, proceduresRich hierarchy for clinical meaning
ICD-9/ICD-10 and national variantsDiagnoses for billing and statisticsCommon in source data; often mapped to SNOMED
LOINCLaboratory tests and observationsIdentifies what was measured
RxNormMedicationsNormalised drugs, ingredients and doses
CPT4, HCPCS and othersProcedures and servicesCommon in US claims data

Medical vocabularies go back centuries; The Book of OHDSI starts with London's Bills of Mortality. Over time each country, system and institution tended to develop its own, which is exactly what makes interoperability and multi-site research hard1.

How OMOP unifies them

The OMOP Standardized Vocabularies consolidate many vocabularies into one common format, refreshed regularly by the OHDSI vocabulary team, and they are mandatory reference tables for every OMOP CDM instance13. Organisations download them from ATHENA, which also offers search across vocabularies; proprietary vocabularies require a licence12.

The key idea is the standard concept. For each clinical meaning, one concept is designated standard and used to record data. The book's example: codes in MeSH, CIEL, SNOMED, ICD-9-CM and Read all describe atrial fibrillation, but only the SNOMED concept is standard; the others are source concepts mapped to it1. Classification concepts, such as MedDRA terms, take part in hierarchies for querying but aren't used to record data1.

Standard designation is decided per domain, not per vocabulary: conditions mainly use SNOMED, measurements SNOMED and LOINC, drugs RxNorm, RxNorm Extension and CVX1. In the book's words, there is no such thing as a "standard vocabulary".

Domains are messier than they look

Every concept is assigned a domain, such as condition, drug, procedure or measurement, which decides which CDM table it lands in. Source vocabularies often mix domains; the book shows that procedure vocabularies like CPT4 and HCPCS contain concepts from several domains1.

Mapping isn't a one-off ETL task. Vocabularies change, concepts are deprecated and remapped, and every refresh can shift results. Version the vocabulary like any other dependency.

Why this matters for health AI

  • Features and cohorts depend on it. A model trained on "diabetes" is only as good as the concept set behind it, as in OMOP cohort definitions.
  • Portability depends on it. A model built on standard concepts can be validated at another site; one built on local codes usually can't.
  • LLMs need grounding. Language models are good at suggesting codes and poor at being reliably right. Constrain them to look up concepts in the vocabulary rather than generate codes from memory, and validate outputs, in the spirit of SHACL validation for knowledge graphs.
  • Hierarchies enable better questions. Querying all descendants of a concept finds patients that a flat code list would miss.

For the architecture around the vocabularies, see FHIR to OMOP and OMOP data quality checks.

item.title: Kubernetes admission policies in CEL: a playbook for retiring your webhooks
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is GA and MutatingAdmissionPolicy reached stable in v1.36. How CEL policies replace admission webhooks, and how I migrate cluster guardrails safely.
item.content:encoded:
Admission webhooks have guarded Kubernetes clusters for years, at the cost of extra services that can slow or break the API server. Kubernetes now has built-in, declarative alternatives for both validation and mutation.

Every mature Kubernetes platform ends up with guardrails: containers must not run as root, images must come from approved registries, every workload needs an owner label, and some defaults should be injected automatically. For years the standard way to enforce them was admission webhooks, separate services the API server calls on every relevant request. They work, but they're more infrastructure to run, they add latency, and a failing webhook can block deployments across a cluster.

Built-in policies, in CEL

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy reached general availability in Kubernetes 1.30. It lets you express validation rules declaratively in Common Expression Language (CEL), evaluated inside the API server, as an alternative to validating webhooks12. The GA announcement walks through replacing a webhook that enforces least-privilege security context settings with an equivalent policy1.

MutatingAdmissionPolicy does the same for changes. The documentation describes it as a declarative, in-process alternative to mutating webhooks, with mutations defined as an apply configuration merged using server-side apply rules, or as a JSON patch3. The feature gate list shows it moving through alpha and beta to stable in v1.364.

A policy is made of a policy resource, a binding that scopes where it applies, and optional parameters, so one policy can be reused with different settings per namespace or environment23.

Webhooks, built-in policies, or a policy engine

Built-in CEL policiesWebhooks or policy engines
Runs whereInside the API serverSeparate services the API server calls
Failure modeNo extra service to go downWebhook outages can block or slow admission
LogicCEL expressions over the request and parametersArbitrary code or rich policy languages
External callsNot designed for themPossible, for example image signature checks
ReportingBasicOften richer reports and policy libraries

My rule of thumb: simple, high-volume guardrails move to built-in policies; checks that need external data or rich reporting stay in a policy engine.

The migration playbook

  1. Inventory webhooks and policies across clusters, including those installed by vendor charts, with their failure policies and timeouts.
  2. Classify each rule: expressible in CEL, needs external data, or needs complex logic.
  3. Write CEL equivalents for the first group, with test cases for allowed and rejected objects, kept in version control alongside your platform code.
  4. Roll out in audit or warn mode first, comparing results with the existing webhook before switching to deny.
  5. Use parameters and bindings to vary settings per environment instead of copying policies.
  6. Remove the old webhook only after the policy has matched its decisions in production for a period.

Every webhook you retire is one less service that can take down deployments at 2am. That operational simplicity is the main benefit, more than any feature.

Guardrails worth having on AI clusters

  • GPU workloads must declare an owner, cost centre and priority class, so costs and preemption are traceable, supporting AI cost allocation.
  • Model-serving pods must not run privileged and must come from approved registries.
  • Namespaces holding regulated data must carry labels that other controls depend on, such as region or data class, as in UAE health data localisation.
  • Training jobs must use the queueing and scheduling setup in Kubernetes gang scheduling rather than bypassing it.

item.title: Team Topologies for AI: where your AI engineers should actually sit
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Should AI engineers form a central team or join product teams? How I use Team Topologies' team types and interaction modes to organise AI work as a fractional CTO.
item.content:encoded:
Most companies building with AI eventually ask the same question: central AI team, or AI engineers in every product team? Team Topologies offers a better answer than either extreme.

The first AI hire is easy. By the fifth, someone usually asks where they should sit. One option is a central AI team that builds everything; it becomes a bottleneck and a queue. The other scatters AI engineers across product teams; each one reinvents model access, evaluation and guardrails, and nobody owns the shared risks. Neither works for long.

A useful vocabulary

Team Topologies, the framework from Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, describes four team types1:

  • Stream-aligned teams deliver value along a flow of work, usually a product or customer journey.
  • Platform teams provide internal services that reduce the load on others.
  • Enabling teams help other teams build new capabilities, for a limited time, then move on.
  • Complicated-subsystem teams own parts that need deep specialist knowledge.

And three ways for teams to interact: collaboration, working closely towards a shared goal, mainly during discovery; X-as-a-Service, consuming what another team provides with minimal coordination; and facilitating, one team helping another learn12. Interactions that fit none of these are often a sign that team boundaries are drawn badly2.

How I map AI work onto it

AI workTeam typeWhy
AI features in a productStream-alignedThe team that owns the journey owns the AI in it, including its quality
Model gateway, evaluation tooling, observability, GPU capacityPlatformShared once, consumed as a service by every product team
Teaching teams to build, evaluate and secure AI featuresEnablingTime-boxed help that leaves capability behind
Custom models, fine-tuning, a governed ontologyComplicated-subsystemGenuinely specialist work that product teams shouldn't carry

The question isn't "central or embedded". It's which AI work is product work, which is platform work, and which is temporary teaching.

Interaction modes over time

The modes should change as capability matures. Early on, an AI platform or enabling team collaborates closely with one or two product teams to discover what's needed. Once patterns stabilise, the platform offers them as a service: an approved gateway, evaluation pipelines, templates. Enabling help moves on to the next team. If a product team still needs constant hand-holding a year later, the platform's interfaces are probably the problem, which is exactly what the platform engineering maturity model helps diagnose.

Conway's law applies to AI too

Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structures3. In AI, the effect is easy to spot: a central AI team produces a central AI service that every product must queue for; fully scattered teams produce five slightly different gateways and no shared evaluation. Design the team structure you want the architecture to reflect.

What I put in place first

  1. Name owners for AI features in each product team, including their evaluation and incident handling.
  2. Create a small AI platform capability for the gateway, evaluation and observability, run as a product with internal users; see LLM model routing and AI cost allocation for what typically lives there.
  3. Time-box enabling work, with explicit exit criteria for each team supported.
  4. Declare interaction modes between teams, so expectations are clear and revisited.
  5. Record the design as an architecture decision record and revisit it each half year.

item.title: pgvector or a dedicated vector database? How I decide for RAG and search
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Postgres with pgvector handles more vector search than many teams expect. What pgvector 0.8 changed for filtered queries, its limits, and when a dedicated vector database is worth it.
item.content:encoded:
Teams starting retrieval-augmented generation often reach for a new database before checking the one they already run. For many workloads, Postgres with pgvector is enough. For some it isn't. Here is how I tell the difference.

A familiar pattern: a team decides to add RAG to its product, evaluates three vector databases, picks one, and six months later is running a second database with its own backups, security reviews, access controls and sync pipeline, all to store a few million embeddings next to data that already lives in Postgres.

Sometimes that's the right call. Often it isn't.

What pgvector gives you

pgvector is an open-source Postgres extension for vector similarity search, supporting exact search as well as approximate indexes such as HNSW and IVFFlat1. The strongest argument for it isn't performance. It's that vectors live beside your relational data, under the same transactions, backups, access controls and operational tooling.

That matters most for filtering. Real RAG queries are rarely "the nearest chunks"; they are "the nearest chunks this user may see, from this tenant, in this product line, updated this year". In Postgres those filters are ordinary SQL against data you already govern.

The filtering problem, and the 0.8 fix

Approximate indexes return a limited candidate set, and filters apply afterwards. With a selective filter, that can leave very few results: the Nile write-up of the release cites an example where a condition matching 10% of rows yields only about four results with default HNSW settings4.

pgvector 0.8.0, released in late 2024, added iterative index scans: if the first pass returns too few matches, the scan continues until it finds enough or hits a configured limit, with options for strict or relaxed ordering23. It also improved cost estimation so the planner makes better index choices when filtering2. The release notes add a useful reminder: where an ordinary index such as a B-tree can meet performance needs, it gives exact results2.

Filtered retrieval is where many RAG systems quietly fail: the right document exists but the user is told nothing relevant was found. Test with your real filters, not unfiltered benchmarks.

How I decide

Favours pgvectorFavours a dedicated vector database
Vectors relate closely to existing relational dataVector search is the main workload, not a feature
Rich filters, permissions and multi-tenancy in SQLVery large collections or very high query rates
Moderate scale that fits your Postgres capacitySearch load would compete with transactional work
Team already runs Postgres wellNeed for features Postgres lacks in your setup
Strong consistency between data and embeddingsIndependent scaling of search from the database

A middle path is common: start on pgvector, measure, and move only the search workload if it outgrows Postgres. If your operational database is MongoDB, the equivalent question applies there, as in hybrid search for RAG on MongoDB.

Practical rules for pgvector

  1. Benchmark with your filters and your data, measuring recall as well as latency.
  2. Enforce permissions in the query, ideally with row-level security, so retrieval can't return documents a user shouldn't see. The same principle applies to tenants, as in multi-tenant SaaS patterns.
  3. Separate search load with read replicas if it begins to affect transactional performance.
  4. Combine with keyword search; Postgres full-text search plus vectors is a reasonable hybrid for many products.
  5. Evaluate retrieval quality with a labelled set, as in the RAG to production checklist, before tuning indexes.

item.title: Evaluating AI agents: why reliability matters more than a single success rate
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Agents that succeed once may fail the next time. What τ-bench and τ²-bench reveal about agent reliability, the pass^k metric, and how I build agent evaluations for production.
item.content:encoded:
An agent demo succeeds because someone ran it until it did. Production runs every task once, for real users, thousands of times. Research on agent benchmarks shows how big that gap can be, and how to measure it.

Many agent evaluations report a single number: "the agent completes 80% of tasks." That number usually comes from running each task once, or from the best of several runs. For a chatbot answering questions, it might be enough. For an agent that changes bookings, issues refunds or updates records, it hides the question that matters: if a customer asks for the same thing ten times, how often does the agent get it right every time?

What τ-bench measures

Sierra's τ-bench put agents in realistic customer service domains. The agent talks to a simulated user, calls domain APIs and must follow a written policy. Success is judged objectively: does the final state of the database match the expected outcome12?

It also introduced pass^k: the probability that an agent succeeds on all k independent attempts at the same task1. That is a reliability measure, unlike pass@k, which asks whether any attempt succeeds. The authors reported that even state-of-the-art function-calling agents at the time succeeded on fewer than half the tasks, and that consistency was worse, with pass^8 below 25% in the retail domain1.

A 60% success rate on one attempt can mean a much lower chance of handling the same request correctly every time. Customers experience the second number.

When users act too

Real support often involves the customer doing things: restarting a device, checking a setting, confirming a code. τ²-bench extended the idea to a dual-control setting where both agent and user use tools to change a shared environment, and reported that performance dropped noticeably when agents moved from no-user settings to dual control34. Guiding a person through a task is a skill of its own, and it needs its own tests.

How I build agent evaluations

  1. Judge outcomes, not transcripts. Wherever possible, check the end state in the system of record, as τ-bench does, rather than asking a model whether the conversation looked right.
  2. Write policies down, then test them. Refund limits, identity checks and escalation rules become explicit test cases, including ones where the right answer is "no".
  3. Simulate users with variety: impatient, confused, adversarial, and users who change their minds. Include prompt injection attempts, as in prompt injection defence.
  4. Run every task several times and report pass^k alongside the single-run rate. Release gates should use the reliability number.
  5. Grow the suite from production. Every incident and escalation becomes a test case, per AI incident postmortems.
  6. Trace everything. Tool calls, arguments and results, so a failing run can be diagnosed; see LLM observability.

This sits on top of the general method in evaluation sets that predict production, with two additions specific to agents: state-based judging and repeated trials.

What to do with the results

Low reliability isn't always a reason to stop. It's a reason to change the design: narrower tools, deterministic code for policy checks, human approval for irreversible actions, and the containment patterns in MCP Apps and tool annotations. Often the best improvement isn't a better model but less for the model to decide.

item.title: The UAE health data law: designing health AI and cloud platforms for localisation
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: UAE health data must generally stay in the country unless an exception applies. What the ICT Health Data Law requires, the 2021 exceptions, and how I architect health AI around it.
item.content:encoded:
Health tech companies entering the UAE often plan around the general data protection law and miss the stricter rule that applies to health data. It shapes where your databases, models and support teams can be.

When health tech companies plan a UAE launch, the conversation usually starts with the federal Personal Data Protection Law, which I covered in UAE PDPL and AI architecture. For health data there is a more specific and stricter rule: the federal law on the use of information and communications technology in health fields, Federal Law No. 2 of 2019. Its localisation requirement is the one that most often changes an architecture.

As always, this is an architect's reading. Confirm the current position and any emirate-level rules with UAE counsel.

The core rule

Article 13 of the law provides that health data relating to health services provided in the UAE cannot be stored, processed, generated or transferred outside the country, unless permitted, such as by a resolution of a health authority in coordination with the Ministry of Health and Prevention14.

In 2021 the Ministry issued a resolution setting out exceptions. Commentary describes ten circumstances, including pharmacovigilance reporting, scientific research, insurance claims administration, and processing in the context of wearables and health monitoring devices23. Qualifying is not automatic: each exception carries conditions that organisations must be able to meet2.

Treat in-country as the default and every cross-border flow as an exception that needs a named legal basis and evidence that its conditions are met.

Where AI and cloud designs trip up

ComponentThe localisation question
Primary database and backupsAre both in a UAE region, including disaster recovery copies?
Model inferenceDoes any prompt containing health data reach a model hosted abroad?
Embeddings and vector storeAre embeddings of clinical text created and stored in the UAE?
Logs, traces and analyticsDo prompts, responses or identifiers land in a foreign observability tool?
Support and engineering accessCan staff abroad view production health data?
Wearables and devicesWhich exception applies, and are its conditions met?

The same hidden-transfer problem I described for Saudi PDPL and cross-border AI applies here, with less room for manoeuvre because the default is stricter.

The architecture I use

  1. A UAE data plane. Databases, object storage, backups, vector stores and analytics in UAE cloud regions or on-premises, with infrastructure policies that block resources elsewhere.
  2. In-country inference for anything touching health data: private models or in-region managed services, following the options in where to run models in the UAE.
  3. A gateway that enforces it, redacting or blocking health data before any call to services outside the country.
  4. Local observability, with a regional OpenTelemetry gateway as in Collector deployment patterns, and metadata-only export if anything must leave.
  5. Access controls by location for support and engineering, with break-glass procedures and logging.
  6. A register of exceptions, mapping any permitted transfer to the specific exception, its conditions and the evidence.

A regional platform

For companies serving several Gulf markets, I design one platform with a data plane per jurisdiction and a shared control plane that never touches patient data. It costs more than a single region, but it is far cheaper than re-platforming after a regulator or a hospital client asks where their data lives.
